0.title: The Magna Carta of Christian Liberty: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians
0.overview:
Paul wrote to the Galatians in a state of controlled fury. He was angry not for himself but for them — and for the gospel. Every other letter he wrote to a church opens with thanksgiving or blessing to God; Galatians has neither. He moves immediately, in the very first verse, to defend his apostolic authority, and by verse 6 he is in open astonishment: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel.” The urgency that presses through every paragraph of this letter was born of Paul’s conviction that the gospel itself was at stake — not a peripheral issue but the very core of what he had preached and what they had received.

The crisis had been created by a group scholars call the Judaizers — Jewish Christians who insisted that faith in Christ was necessary but not sufficient. Gentile believers also needed to be circumcised and observe the Mosaic law in order to be fully accepted by God and fully included in God’s people. This seems, on the surface, like a minor addition: faith in Christ plus a few religious practices. But Paul saw it with total clarity for what it was: a fundamental contradiction of the gospel. If anything in addition to Christ is required for justification — even something God-given and ancient like circumcision — then Christ is no longer sufficient, grace is no longer free, and the cross is no longer enough. “If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose” (2:21).

Where were these churches, and when did Paul write? Galatia was both an ethnic region in the north of Asia Minor, settled by Celtic tribes, and a Roman province that also took in the southern cities of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Some think Paul wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, whom he may have visited on his later journeys (Acts 16:6; 18:23), and date the letter in the mid-50s. The more likely reading is that he wrote to the southern churches he founded on his first journey (Acts 13–14): Paul normally used the Roman provincial names, and Acts tells us plainly about those churches and nothing about any in the north. On that reading the letter was written around AD 48, just before the Jerusalem Council, which would explain why Paul never mentions the Council’s decision (cf. 2:1). It may well be his earliest letter. Its message does not depend on the answer.

Galatians is structured in three movements. Chapters 1–2 are autobiographical: Paul defends the divine origin of his gospel (he received it not from men but from Jesus Christ directly) and recounts his confrontation with Peter at Antioch, where the gospel’s logic was at stake in a table-fellowship dispute. Chapters 3–4 are theological: Paul argues from Scripture (Abraham, the covenant, the law’s purpose, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah) that the gospel of grace by faith preceded the Mosaic law by 430 years and is not superseded by it. Chapters 5–6 are practical: the freedom of the gospel is not license for the flesh but the only true basis for life in the Spirit and love for the neighbor.

Martin Luther’s Commentary on Galatians (1535) is among the most celebrated commentaries in the history of the church. He called this letter his “Katie von Bora” — his beloved, the one he was married to. For Luther, Galatians was the text that articulated what the Reformation was about: the righteousness of God is not a demanding standard to be met but a free gift to be received. Justification is by faith alone, in Christ alone, by grace alone. Anything added to that formula is a subtraction from it.

Read Galatians as the most passionate defense of free grace in the entire canon. Every person who has ever felt that their standing before God depends on their performance needs to hear it. Every church that has drifted toward moralism — toward making the Christian life about spiritual self-improvement rather than trust in the finished work of Christ — needs to be dragged back to Galatians and made to sit with it until the gospel is clear again. Paul wrote it because the gospel is always under threat, and the threat almost always comes from the same direction: the desire to add something to Christ, to make grace a little less free, to make human effort a little more decisive. Galatians says: no. The cross is enough. Christ is enough. Grace is enough. “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

1.title: No Other Gospel: The Divine Origin of Paul’s Message
1.overview:
The letter begins with a defense of apostolic authority and immediately escalates to a declaration that would have shocked its first hearers: the gospel Paul preached is not of human origin, and anyone — even an angel from heaven — who preaches a different gospel is under divine curse. The word translated “accursed” is anathema — the strongest possible language of divine condemnation. Paul uses it twice in two verses (vv. 8–9), the repetition signaling that this is not rhetorical heat but deliberate, settled conviction.

The reason for the severity is simple: if the gospel can be modified by human authority — by apostles, by tradition, by ecclesiastical consensus — then it is not the gospel of God but the gospel of men. And the gospel of men, however sincerely presented, however religiously decorated, cannot save. Only the gospel that comes from God can bring a person into right standing with God. The divine origin of the gospel is therefore not an abstract theological claim; it is the practical ground of the gospel’s saving power.

Paul then makes his case autobiographically. He was not taught the gospel by the Jerusalem apostles; he received it directly from Jesus Christ, by revelation. The account of his conversion and his minimal contact with the Jerusalem church in the years that followed is not self-congratulation but an argument: his gospel is independently and divinely authenticated. It is the same gospel the Jerusalem apostles preach — but its authority does not rest on their endorsement. It rests on the revelation of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by stressing that his apostleship came not from any human source or appointment but directly from Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, the very point his opponents in Galatia disputed. Writing with the believers around him to the churches of Galatia, he wishes them grace and peace from God and from Christ, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, as the Father willed, and he gives glory to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as Eternal Initiative, Not Emergency Repair

The christological formula of vv. 3–5 is among the earliest in the New Testament, and it grounds the Reformed conviction that salvation originates wholly in God. The Son’s self-giving is voluntary; its object is our sins; its effect is rescue out of an age, not improvement within it; and its source is the Father’s own will. Two errors are shut out at once. The first makes the cross a late correction to a plan that went wrong — but Christ gave himself according to the will of our God and Father, and Peter preaches the same thing at Pentecost, that he was delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

The second sets a stern Father against a merciful Son, as though mercy had to be extracted from heaven by the death of Jesus. Verse 4 forbids it. The Father willed the giving; the Son gave himself; there is no division of sentiment in the Trinity toward sinners. Grace is not reactive. It is eternal initiative, and it terminates in glory to God (v. 5), which is where the letter will end up as well.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had received a complete gospel and were being told it was a foundation needing a second storey. Paul’s opening answers that before it is raised: the apostleship is unmediated (v. 1), the senders are a company and not a maverick (v. 2), and the gospel summarised in vv. 3–5 has no vacancy in it for a human contribution — Christ gave himself, and the Father willed it.

Now: The same instinct survives wherever the gospel is treated as the entry requirement and something else as the real content of the Christian life — a sacramental record, a moral achievement, an intensity of spiritual experience. The test is simple and can be run on a bad week: if approaching God after a week of failure feels materially different from approaching him after a good one, something has already been added, whatever is said out loud.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead— and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:

Meaning first. Galatians is Paul’s most urgent letter, written to defend the heart of the gospel: that sinners are justified before God by faith in Christ alone, not by keeping the law of Moses. After Paul planted churches in Galatia, teachers came insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law to be truly saved. Chapter 1 sets the stage. Paul’s greeting already stresses that his apostleship came directly from Christ, and that Christ gave himself for our sins to rescue us (vv. 1–5). Instead of his usual thanksgiving, Paul expresses astonishment that they are turning to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all, and pronounces a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches another (vv. 6–10). Then he begins a long defence of his gospel’s divine origin: he received it not from any human being but by revelation from Jesus Christ. His former life as a zealous persecutor, his sudden call by grace, and his independence from the Jerusalem apostles in the years after his conversion all prove it (vv. 11–24). The Galatians must not abandon a gospel that came from God.

Setting and background. Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Many think Paul wrote to the southern Galatian churches he planted on his first missionary journey: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13–14), perhaps around AD 48–49, before the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15, which made Galatians perhaps his earliest letter. Others think he wrote to ethnic Galatians in the north, later, around AD 55. The message is the same either way.

Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man. Key words. Not from men: his apostleship did not originate with any human authority. Nor through man: no human was the channel of his appointment. The false teachers probably claimed Paul was a second-hand apostle, dependent on Jerusalem.

But through Jesus Christ and God the Father. Key words. Christ commissioned him directly on the Damascus road (Acts 9:15; 26:16–18). Notice Christ is named alongside the Father as the source of apostolic authority: Christ is not merely human.

Who raised him from the dead. Key words. The risen Christ appointed Paul. The resurrection is God’s seal on Christ’s work.

And all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia. Key words. Several churches in the region. No warm words of praise follow, unlike other letters. The situation is too serious.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul rejected all human fellowship or accountability. He later consulted the Jerusalem apostles (2:2). It means his message did not depend on their approval.

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle sent not by human beings or through any human agency, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and from all the brothers and sisters with him, to the churches in Galatia:

On a Tuesday. The gospel you believe did not come from human invention. It came from God. Hold it firmly.
verseByVerse.note: Galatia was a Roman province in central Asia Minor. Many think the letter went to the churches Paul founded on his first journey — Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe; others think of ethnic Galatians farther north.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Grace: God’s free, undeserved favour, the theme of the letter. Peace: the wholeness that comes from being right with God.

Who gave himself for our sins. Key words. The gospel in a phrase. Christ gave himself: voluntarily, as a sacrifice. For our sins: to atone for them, in our place (1 Corinthians 15:3). Not our works but his self-giving deals with sin. The false teachers were adding law-keeping to this.

To deliver us from the present evil age. Key words. “Deliver” (exaireō, rescue, snatch out). The present evil age: this world under sin, Satan and death (Ephesians 2:2). Christ has rescued us into the age to come, which has already begun in him. The law belonged to the old age; going back to it is going back to bondage.

According to the will of our God and Father. Key words. The cross was the Father’s plan.

To whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen. Key words. Salvation by grace gives all glory to God. Salvation by works would share the glory with us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are taken out of the world now. They are rescued from its power while still living in it (John 17:15).

In a sentence. Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

For worship. Christ gave himself for your sins. Give the glory to God for it, forever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Instead of thanksgiving, Paul expresses astonishment that the Galatians are so quickly turning from the God who called them by grace to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all, only a distortion spread by people unsettling them. Anyone who preaches a gospel contrary to the one they received, even Paul himself or an angel, is under God’s curse; he says it twice. He is not trying to win human approval; if he were, he would not be Christ’s servant.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Stands Over the Church That Preaches It

The double anathema of vv. 8–9 establishes something the Reformers staked their lives on: the gospel is not the church’s property, to be developed by councils or refined by consensus. A message that human authority conferred can be amended by human authority, and would be. Paul therefore submits himself and heaven’s own courier to the same test he asks the Galatians to apply, which is not the prestige of the teacher but conformity to what was first delivered. Luther read these two verses and recognised the whole controversy of his century in them.

It should be added, because Paul’s own practice requires it, that the curse is not aimed at every disagreement among Christians: he allows real latitude on food and days and disputable matters (Rom. 14). What cannot be renegotiated is the ground of acceptance with God. And the reason nobody may edit this gospel is that it was bought, not drafted — there was an anathema in this story before Paul used the word, and it fell on the Son, becoming a curse for us (3:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were very probably sincere, and would have described themselves as the conservative party taking the Old Testament seriously. Circumcision was God’s own ordinance; the law was divinely given. They were not conscious apostates but well-meaning teachers who had inverted the relationship of law and grace — which is exactly why v. 10 matters, since sincerity was never the test.

Now: A different gospel rarely announces itself as one. It presents as the fuller, more serious, more culturally credible version. Two questions from this passage sort it out. Does this teaching change the ground on which a sinner is accepted by God, or only a secondary matter Christians have long disagreed about? And for a reader with a mother or a brother in such a church, the pastoral answer is in the grammar of vv. 8–9: the anathema falls on the one preaching, not on the sheep being misled.

verseByVerse.quote: I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel— not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.

I am astonished. Key words. “Astonished” (thaumazō, amazed, shocked). In other letters, Paul begins with thanksgiving. Here, nothing to thank God for: only shock.

That you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ. Key words. “Deserting” (metatithēmi, changing sides, a word used of military deserters or political turncoats). Present tense: they are in the act of deserting. And they are deserting not just a message but God himself, who called them. So quickly: soon after their conversion, or soon after the false teachers arrived.

And are turning to a different gospel. Key words. “Different” (heteros, another of a different kind).

Not that there is another one. Key words. “Another” (allos, another of the same kind). There is only one gospel. A different message is not good news at all.

But there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ. Key words. Teachers had come insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved (Acts 15:1, 5). “Trouble” (tarassō, stir up, unsettle). “Distort” (metastrephō, turn around, reverse). Adding law-keeping to faith in Christ does not improve the gospel; it reverses it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the false teachers denied Christ entirely. They added to him. That is precisely what makes it another gospel: Christ plus something.

In a sentence. Paul is astonished that you are so quickly deserting the one who called you to live in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel, which is really no gospel at all. Evidently some people are throwing you into confusion and are trying to pervert the gospel of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Watch for subtle additions to the gospel: Christ plus church attendance, Christ plus rules, Christ plus good works. The gospel is Christ alone.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers had come insisting that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.

But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you. Key words. The authority lies in the message, not the messenger. Even Paul himself, or an angel, would be wrong if they changed the gospel. This rules out new revelations that contradict the apostolic gospel, whether claimed by angels (as in some later religions) or by church authorities.

Let him be accursed. Key words. “Accursed” is anathema: handed over to God’s judgement, devoted to destruction. The strongest condemnation possible. A false gospel destroys souls.

As we have said before, so now I say again. Key words. Repeated for emphasis, and perhaps referring to warnings given when Paul was with them.

If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed. Key words. The test is the gospel they received: the apostolic gospel, now preserved in Scripture.

Where Christians differ: how serious is false teaching? Many today treat doctrinal differences as unimportant, as long as people are sincere. Verdict: Paul shows that changing the gospel itself, especially adding works to faith as the ground of justification, is a matter of eternal life and death. Not every disagreement is a matter of the gospel; Christians may differ charitably on secondary matters (Romans 14). But on the way of salvation, there is no room for compromise. Justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone is the article on which the church stands or falls.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may curse people personally. Paul pronounces God’s judgement on those who corrupt the gospel. Our response to false teachers is to warn, refute and pray for their repentance.

In a sentence. But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach a gospel other than the one we preached to you, let them be under God’s curse! As we have already said, so now Paul says again: if anybody is preaching to you a gospel other than what you accepted, let them be under God’s curse!

For worship. Thank God for the true gospel. Pray that your church will guard it faithfully.
verseByVerse.note: “Accursed” is anathema — handed over to God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.

For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Key words. The opponents accused Paul of watering down the gospel for Gentiles, dropping circumcision to make it easier and win followers. Paul answers: does a man who pronounces curses sound like a people-pleaser?

Or am I trying to please man? Key words. “Please” (areskō).

If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ. Key words. “Still”: as he did in his former life, when he sought the approval of his Jewish teachers. “Servant” (doulos, slave). You cannot serve two masters. A slave of Christ lives for his master’s approval.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about people. He became all things to all people to save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). But he never changed the message to please them.

In a sentence. Is Paul now trying to win the approval of human beings, or of God? Or is he trying to please people? If he were still trying to please people, he would not be a servant of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Whose approval do you most want today? Live for Christ’s.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now argues from his own biography, and the argument is chronological. In vv. 11–12 he states the thesis: the gospel he preached is not man’s gospel; he did not receive it from any man, nor was he taught it. Those two verbs are the exact vocabulary of rabbinic transmission, the machinery that had made him a Pharisee, and he is saying it had nothing to do with this. (When he tells Corinth that he received and delivered the resurrection facts, there is no contradiction: the facts came from the church, the meaning and the commission came by revelation of Jesus Christ.)

Then the evidence. Verses 13–14 are his own record of shame produced as an exhibit: he persecuted the church beyond measure and tried to destroy it, the verb an army uses of a city it means to leave uninhabitable — and he was advancing beyond his peers, ahead of many of his own age, winning at the system he was in. Nobody defects from the top of a religion he is succeeding at into a message that gets him flogged. In vv. 15–16 the sentence turns and every verb becomes God’s: set me apart before I was born (before there was a person there to be good or bad), called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son — God’s delight, not his duty — and the commission to the Gentiles arrives in the same breath as the conversion.

The rest is a chronology of distance. Verse 17 has him going not to Jerusalem but to Arabia, the Nabatean kingdom, where he was evidently preaching hard enough to make an enemy of a king (2 Cor. 11:32–33). Verses 18–19 give the numbers that carry the argument: after three years, fifteen days, two men — and the verb translated visit means to get to know someone, not to be trained or certified by them.

Verse 20 breaks off into an oath, which tells us Paul was not merely disagreed with but called a liar. Verses 21–22 put him in Syria and Cilicia — home to Tarsus, and several years with nothing recorded — still unknown in person, literally unknown by face, to the very Judean churches he had once hunted. And vv. 23–24 close with the one sentence those churches kept repeating: he who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy. Their response was not to check his credentials. They glorified God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Election, Effectual Calling, and Revelation: the Grammar of Grace

Verses 15–16 are among the most compact statements of sovereign grace in Paul. Three divine acts stand in order, and Paul initiates none of them: God set him apart before birth, called him by grace, and was pleased to reveal his Son in him. The setting apart echoes Jeremiah called before the womb and the Servant of Isaiah 49; there may also be a deliberate play on words, since aphorizō, to set apart, sounds against the name Pharisee, most likely from a root meaning the separated ones.

Paul had separated himself by rigorous effort and it made him dangerous; God had set him apart before he separated himself from anything, and set him apart for the Gentiles. The calling is effectual, not an invitation awaiting a reply — the last thing Saul intended on that road was conversion. And the revelation is in me, internal as well as external: he had known the facts about Jesus for years and hated them. Grace that reaches a man riding in the opposite direction with warrants in his bag is not a reward for seeking. (cf. Rom. 8:29–30; Eph. 1:4–5)
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul’s critics could point to his absence from Jesus’ earthly ministry and his late arrival among the apostles. His reply is the chronology of vv. 17–22: he went to Arabia rather than Jerusalem, waited three years, stayed a fortnight, met two men, then vanished into Cilicia for years, and the Judean churches would not have recognised him in the street. If his gospel came from that world, its members would at least have known his face.

Now: A disqualifying history made into evidence (vv. 13–14), a calling that began before the one called was looking (v. 15), and hidden years that turn out to be part of the work (vv. 17, 21–22) — three things that reach an ordinary believer directly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel. Key words. Not of human origin. Literally, not according to man: not shaped by human thinking.

For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it. Key words. Paul did not get his gospel from tradition or teachers, as rabbis received the law from their masters.

But I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ. Key words. “Revelation” (apokalypsis, unveiling). Christ himself revealed it to Paul, on the Damascus road and afterwards. “Of Jesus Christ” can mean from Christ, or about Christ: both are true.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul learned no facts about Jesus from others. He received historical tradition (1 Corinthians 15:3). It means the gospel itself, its meaning and his commission, came directly from Christ.

In a sentence. Paul wants you to know, brothers and sisters, that the gospel he preached is not of human origin. He did not receive it from any person, nor was he taught it; rather, he received it by revelation from Jesus Christ.

For worship. The gospel came from Christ himself. Receive it as his word, not human opinion.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.

For you have heard of my former life in Judaism. Key words. Paul’s story was well known. Judaism: the Jewish religion and way of life.

How I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it. Key words. “Violently” (kath’ hyperbolēn, beyond measure). “Destroy” (portheō, ravage, as an army sacks a city). He arrested, imprisoned and voted for the deaths of believers (Acts 8:3; 22:4; 26:10–11). Notice: the church of God. He was fighting God.

And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people. Key words. He was a rising star, trained under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3).

So extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers. Key words. “Zealous” (zēlōtēs). The traditions: the oral law of the Pharisees (Mark 7:3). The point: no human could have converted such a man. Nothing in his background would have led him to the gospel of grace. Only a revelation from God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean zeal is bad. It means zeal for the wrong cause is deadly.

In a sentence. For you have heard of Paul’s previous way of life in Judaism, how intensely he persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it. He was advancing in Judaism beyond many of his own age among his people and was extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers.

On a Tuesday. No one is too far from God to be saved. Pray for the most hostile unbeliever you know.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;

But when he who had set me apart before I was born. Key words. “Set apart” (aphorizō, separate, appoint). Literally, from my mother’s womb. Like Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and the Servant (Isaiah 49:1). God chose Paul before he had done anything, good or bad. Election is prior to everything.

And who called me by his grace. Key words. The effective call on the Damascus road. By grace: Paul deserved the opposite.

Was pleased to reveal his Son to me. Key words. “Was pleased” (eudokeō, delighted): God’s good pleasure. “To me” is literally in me: an inward revelation as well as an outward vision (2 Corinthians 4:6).

In order that I might preach him among the Gentiles. Key words. His commission was given at his conversion (Acts 9:15; 26:17–18).

I did not immediately consult with anyone. Key words. Literally, I did not confer with flesh and blood. He did not go to human authorities for interpretation or approval.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was a loner. Ananias ministered to him (Acts 9:17). It means his gospel did not depend on human instruction.

In a sentence. But when God, who set Paul apart from his mother’s womb and called him by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son in him so that he might preach him among the Gentiles, Paul did not consult any human being.

For worship. If you are a believer, God set you apart and called you by his grace, long before you knew him. Praise him.

parallels.desc: the LORD called me from the womb

verseByVerse.quote: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.

Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me. Key words. He did not go to the Twelve for authorisation. “Before me”: they were apostles earlier, but not higher.

But I went away into Arabia. Key words. Arabia here is the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus, ruled by King Aretas (2 Corinthians 11:32). Why Arabia? Perhaps for reflection and prayer, rethinking the Scriptures in the light of Christ; perhaps to preach, which would explain why Aretas’s governor later wanted to arrest him. Some connect it with Mount Sinai, also in Arabia (4:25), as Elijah went there (1 Kings 19:8).

And returned again to Damascus. Key words. Where he preached boldly until a plot forced him to flee (Acts 9:19–25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Acts is wrong in not mentioning Arabia. Acts 9:23 says “after many days,” leaving room for it.

In a sentence. He did not go up to Jerusalem to see those who were apostles before him, but he went into Arabia. Later he returned to Damascus.

On a Tuesday. Time alone with God and his word shaped Paul. Make space for it in your life.
verseByVerse.note: Arabia here is the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.

Then after three years. Key words. Three years after his conversion, about AD 35–36.

I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas. Key words. Cephas is Peter. “Visit” (historeō, to get to know, to inquire, from which history). He went to get acquainted, perhaps to learn about Jesus’ earthly ministry from an eyewitness, not to receive his gospel.

And remained with him fifteen days. Key words. A short visit, not a long training.

But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother. Key words. James the Lord’s brother led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; 21:18). He was a half-brother of Jesus, converted after the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:7). Paul is careful to show he had minimal contact with the Jerusalem leaders.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul avoided the other apostles. They were probably elsewhere. It means he was not their student.

In a sentence. Then after three years, he went up to Jerusalem to get acquainted with Peter and stayed with him fifteen days. He saw none of the other apostles, only James, the Lord’s brother.

For worship. Thank God for the fellowship of believers who share the same gospel, even across distances.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. James the Lord’s brother led the church in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: (In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)

(In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!) Key words. A solemn oath. The opponents were apparently spreading a different version of Paul’s history: that he had been taught and authorised by Jerusalem and then departed from their teaching. Paul swears before God that his account is true.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may swear casually. Paul uses an oath for a matter of great importance (Matthew 5:33–37 forbids careless or deceptive oaths).

In a sentence. Paul assures you before God that what he is writing to you is no lie.

On a Tuesday. Speak the truth as before God, always.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.

Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. Key words. Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus, where he was born (Acts 9:30; 22:3). Syria included Antioch. He spent about ten years there, preaching, before Barnabas brought him to Antioch (Acts 11:25–26).

And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ. Key words. The Judean churches did not know his face. So he could not have been their student or representative.

What it does not mean. It does not mean he was idle. He was preaching (v. 23).

In a sentence. Then he went to Syria and Cilicia. He was personally unknown to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.

For worship. God uses hidden years of faithful service. Do not despise your quiet seasons.
verseByVerse.note: Cilicia was Paul’s home province, with its capital at Tarsus.

verseByVerse.quote: They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they glorified God because of me.

They only were hearing it said. Key words. The Judean believers knew Paul only by reputation.

“He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” Key words. The news that spread: the persecutor has become a preacher. “The faith”: the gospel, the content of what is believed.

And they glorified God because of me. Key words. The Jerusalem churches did not oppose Paul’s gospel; they praised God for it. A sharp contrast with the false teachers in Galatia. If the Judean believers glorified God for Paul’s ministry, how can the Galatians reject it?

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul sought their praise. They praised God, not Paul.

In a sentence. They only heard the report: “The man who formerly persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.” And they praised God because of him.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of someone’s dramatic conversion, give God the glory. And let your own life give others reason to glorify God.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—<sup>2</sup>and all the brothers who are with me, To the churches of Galatia:<sup>3</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>4</sup>who gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,<sup>5</sup>to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.<sup>6</sup>I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel—<sup>7</sup>not that there is another one, but there are some who trouble you and want to distort the gospel of Christ.<sup>8</sup>But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed.<sup>9</sup>As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone is preaching to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be accursed.<sup>10</sup>For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? Or am I trying to please man? If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.<sup>11</sup>For I would have you know, brothers, that the gospel that was preached by me is not man’s gospel.<sup>12</sup>For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.<sup>13</sup>For you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it.<sup>14</sup>And I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers.<sup>15</sup>But when he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace,<sup>16</sup>was pleased to reveal his Son to me, in order that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with anyone;<sup>17</sup>nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.<sup>18</sup>Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas and remained with him fifteen days.<sup>19</sup>But I saw none of the other apostles except James the Lord’s brother.<sup>20</sup>(In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!)<sup>21</sup>Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.<sup>22</sup>And I was still unknown in person to the churches of Judea that are in Christ.<sup>23</sup>They only were hearing it said, “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.”<sup>24</sup>And they glorified God because of me.

2.title: Justified by Faith: The Gospel Confronts the Church
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is the biographical argument’s climax and the letter’s theological turning point. Two episodes dominate: the Jerusalem conference (vv. 1–10), where the apostles affirmed Paul’s gospel of grace without requiring Gentile circumcision; and the Antioch confrontation (vv. 11–14), where Paul opposed Peter to his face because Peter’s behavior contradicted the gospel he believed. Both episodes illustrate the same point: the gospel of justification by faith alone is the non-negotiable centre of Christianity, and it must be defended even when the offender is the most respected leader in the church.

The chapter’s second half (vv. 15–21) is the theological centrepiece of the entire letter — the most concentrated statement of justification by faith in Paul’s letters apart from Romans 3. “A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” The verb “justified” (dikaioō) is a forensic term: to be declared righteous by the divine judge, to have one’s legal status before God established as “not guilty.” This declaration is made not on the basis of law-keeping (which can only expose and condemn sin) but on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ.

The chapter ends with the most luminous personal testimony in Paul’s letters: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” This is the gospel arriving at its destination: not merely a changed legal status but a transformed life — union with Christ, the old self crucified, the new life animated by faith in the one who loved and gave himself for me, personally, individually, sacrificially.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Paul Accepted by the Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 opens with a number that is itself the argument: after fourteen years of preaching and planting without Jerusalem laying a hand on his message. He goes up with Barnabas, who had once vouched for him when the Jerusalem church would not go near him, and with Titus, an uncircumcised Greek — not a companion so much as an exhibit. In v. 2 he goes because of a revelation, not by summons, and meets the leaders privately rather than staging a public showdown he could have won.

His stated purpose, to make sure he was not “running in vain,” is easily misread as doubt about his gospel; chapter 1 forbids that. The danger he is guarding against is that the church might become two churches, a circumcised one and an uncircumcised one, each with its own apostle and its own terms.

Verse 3 gives the verdict in one line: even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. With the test case standing in the room, Jerusalem did not require him to become a Jew. Verses 4–5 explain the pressure that made this a fight. The language is the language of espionage — false brothers secretly brought in, men who slipped in to spy out the freedom of the Gentile churches, whose stated object was slavery. Paul did not yield even for a moment, and gives a pastoral reason rather than a principled one: so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. Doctrinal firmness is a man standing in a doorway so that people behind him can stay free.

Verse 6 reports the outcome in a phrase — they added nothing to me — and grounds it in the fact that God shows no partiality, a principle Paul turns on the apostles themselves. Verses 7–8 set out the shape of the agreement: Paul entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised just as Peter to the circumcised, one gospel and two mission fields, with God himself named as the one who worked through both men. In v. 9 the order of the clauses carries the theology: the pillars first perceived the grace that was given and only then gave the right hand of fellowship — recognition of what God had done, not a handshake that conferred it. And v. 10 adds the single request Jerusalem made, that they remember the poor, which Paul was already eager to do.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Gospel, One People, One Way In

The Titus decision of v. 3 settles a question of the first order: justification is on identical terms for Jew and Gentile, and no covenant marker supplements faith at the point of acceptance with God. This is not a statement about cultural inclusion; it is a claim about the nature of justification itself, and the Reformed understanding of the covenant of grace — one covenant, one people, one Saviour, one way of entry — finds its clearest apostolic expression here.

Two further principles sit inside the passage. The word entrusted (v. 7) is a steward’s word, and it quietly disqualifies everyone in the dispute from editing the message: Paul may not adjust it to suit Gentiles and Jerusalem may not adjust it to suit Jews, for the same reason, which is that neither owns it. And the sequence of v. 9 — grace perceived, then fellowship extended — gives the church its permanent task in recognising anyone. Ordination does not manufacture a minister and a handshake does not manufacture a brother. The church perceives what God has given and says so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Galatia was being told that Gentile believers needed circumcision added to their faith. Paul’s answer is that he took this precise question to Jerusalem with an uncircumcised Greek at his side (vv. 1–3), and the men whose authority the Judaizers were invoking added nothing (v. 6) and shook his hand (v. 9). The Judaizers are not following the Jerusalem apostles; they are contradicting them.

Now: Anything may be done for the gospel; nothing may be added to it — which is why Paul could later circumcise Timothy (Acts 16:3) and would not let anyone touch Titus. The same test still sorts real questions from false ones. Where a practice is offered as helpful, Christians may differ; where it is required for full acceptance, the gospel is at stake. And v. 10 guards the other flank: having refused to add one item to the gospel, Paul accepts an obligation to the poor without a murmur, because that is not an addition but what grace does once it has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up because of a revelation and set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain.

Meaning first. Galatians 2 completes Paul’s defence of his gospel and states it in its clearest form. First, on a later visit to Jerusalem, Paul laid his gospel before the leading apostles. They added nothing to it, did not require the Gentile Titus to be circumcised, and gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, recognising that God had sent Peter to the Jews and Paul to the Gentiles (vv. 1–10). Second, at Antioch, Peter himself, under pressure from Jewish believers, stopped eating with Gentile Christians. Paul opposed him publicly, because his conduct denied the gospel: if Gentiles are accepted by faith, they cannot be required to live like Jews (vv. 11–14). Third, Paul states the gospel: a person is justified not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. To return to the law as a way of righteousness would rebuild what Christ tore down. Paul has died to the law and been crucified with Christ; Christ now lives in him, and he lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him and gave himself for him. If righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing (vv. 15–21).

Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas. Key words. Fourteen years after his conversion, or after the first visit. It is debated whether this visit is the famine visit of Acts 11:27–30 or the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15. The famine visit fits better if Galatians was written before the Council; the Council fits the subject matter.

Taking Titus along with me. Key words. A Gentile convert, deliberately brought as a test case.

I went up because of a revelation. Key words. God told him to go, not the Jerusalem apostles summoning him. Perhaps the prophecy of Agabus (Acts 11:28).

And set before them (though privately before those who seemed influential) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles. Key words. A private meeting with the leaders, to avoid public controversy.

In order to make sure I was not running or had not run in vain. Key words. Not that Paul doubted his gospel, but that if Jerusalem rejected it, the unity of the church and his work among the Gentiles would be gravely damaged.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul needed Jerusalem’s approval for his gospel to be true. He sought unity, not permission.

In a sentence. Then after fourteen years, Paul went up again to Jerusalem, this time with Barnabas. He took Titus along too. He went in response to a revelation and, meeting privately with those esteemed as leaders, presented to them the gospel that he preaches among the Gentiles. He wanted to be sure he was not running and had not been running his race in vain.

On a Tuesday. Seek unity with fellow believers on the gospel. It is worth the effort.
verseByVerse.note: It is debated whether this visit is the famine visit of Acts 11 or the Jerusalem Council of Acts 15.

verseByVerse.quote: But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery— to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in—who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might bring us into slavery—to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.

But even Titus, who was with me, was not forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. Key words. Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised: a test case for whether Gentile believers must keep the law. The Jerusalem apostles did not require it. This settles the Galatian question.

Yet because of false brothers secretly brought in. Key words. “False brothers” (pseudadelphoi): they claimed to be Christians but were not. “Secretly brought in” (pareisaktos, smuggled in).

Who slipped in to spy out our freedom that we have in Christ Jesus. Key words. Like spies infiltrating an enemy camp. Freedom: from the law as a way of justification, and from its ceremonies.

So that they might bring us into slavery. Key words. Slavery to the law (4:9; 5:1). Adding circumcision as a requirement enslaves.

To them we did not yield in submission even for a moment. Key words. Not for an hour. On the gospel, no compromise.

So that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you. Key words. Paul fought for the Galatians’ sake. The truth of the gospel: the gospel in its true meaning, free grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was always inflexible. He circumcised Timothy for missionary reasons (Acts 16:3), because it was not required for salvation. With Titus, it was demanded as necessary, so he refused.

In a sentence. Yet not even Titus, who was with Paul, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek. This matter arose because some false believers had infiltrated our ranks to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus and to make us slaves. We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you.

For worship. Thank God for the freedom you have in Christ. Guard it against anyone who would add requirements to grace.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek, uncircumcised — a test case for whether Gentile believers must be circumcised.

verseByVerse.quote: And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),
verseByVerse.commentary:
And from those who seemed to be influential (what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality)—those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles),

And from those who seemed to be influential. Key words. The Jerusalem leaders. “Seemed” (dokeō, were reputed). Paul is not mocking them, but noting that the false teachers made much of their reputation.

(What they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality). Key words. Whatever status they had, as companions of the earthly Jesus or relatives, does not matter. God does not judge by appearances (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34).

Those, I say, who seemed influential added nothing to me. Key words. They did not correct or supplement Paul’s gospel. It was complete.

On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel to the circumcised. Key words. One gospel, two mission fields. Peter mainly to Jews, Paul mainly to Gentiles.

(For he who worked through Peter for his apostolic ministry to the circumcised worked also through me for mine to the Gentiles). Key words. The same God was at work in both. The evidence of Paul’s apostleship was God’s work through him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there are two gospels, one for Jews and one for Gentiles. One gospel, different audiences.

In a sentence. As for those who were held in high esteem, whatever they were makes no difference to Paul, for God does not show favouritism; they added nothing to his message. On the contrary, they recognised that he had been entrusted with the task of preaching the gospel to the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been to the circumcised. For God, who was at work in Peter as an apostle to the circumcised, was also at work in Paul as an apostle to the Gentiles.

For worship. Thank God that he works through different people in different places, all with the one gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, perceived the grace that was given to me, they gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.

And when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars. Key words. Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church (Revelation 3:12). James the Lord’s brother, Peter, and John the son of Zebedee.

Perceived the grace that was given to me. Key words. They recognised God’s grace in Paul’s calling and ministry.

They gave the right hand of fellowship to Barnabas and me. Key words. A public sign of agreement and partnership (koinōnia). Full acceptance.

That we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. Key words. A division of labour, not of gospel.

Only, they asked us to remember the poor. Key words. The poor believers in Jerusalem. The only request. Not the law, but love.

The very thing I was eager to do. Key words. Paul was already committed to it, as the later collection showed (2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15:25–27).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not preach to Jews or Peter to Gentiles. Both did. It was a primary focus.

In a sentence. James, Peter and John, those esteemed as pillars, gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship when they recognised the grace given to him. They agreed that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised. All they asked was that we should continue to remember the poor, the very thing Paul had been eager to do all along.

On a Tuesday. Remember the poor. It is one of the marks of gospel faithfulness.
verseByVerse.note: Pillars held up a building; these three were the leaders of the Jerusalem church. The poor were the believers in Judea.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recounts how he confronted Peter at Antioch. Peter had been eating freely with Gentile believers, but when men came from James he drew back and separated himself, afraid of the circumcision party, and other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed his lead in this pretence. Paul saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, so he challenged Peter publicly: if you, a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you force Gentiles to live like Jews?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel Governs the Feet, Not Only the Confession

Peter’s failure was not doctrinal. He had proclaimed the equality of Jew and Gentile before God and won the argument for it. What v. 14 exposes is a gap between a confession genuinely held and a life not walking in line with it — which is what hypocrisy means in Paul’s usage, not the cynical pretence of faith one does not have. The Reformers’ principle that the church is always to be reformed by the gospel bites here: the gospel must govern table habits, social pressure and power dynamics, not merely statements of faith.

There is a further point of some weight. Peter is treated in this passage as a fallible man who can be publicly withstood and corrected by another apostle on a matter of the gospel — and Scripture records it without embarrassment. Whatever authority the Jerusalem leadership had, it was never authority over the message, which is precisely the argument of vv. 6–9.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter’s withdrawal at Antioch was socially motivated, not theologically: v. 12 says he feared the circumcision party. It is the same snare Paul named at 1:10 — am I trying to please man? — and it swept up the whole Jewish contingent and Barnabas with it (v. 13).

Now:Two things in this section reach a reader directly: the room in which he is a slightly different Christian, and the question of when a leader should be confronted in public. Paul’s case meets every condition at once — public conduct, the gospel itself at stake, others being carried away, and the rebuke spoken to Peter’s face rather than about him — and the friendship survived it (2 Pet. 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles; but when they came he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party.

But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face. Key words. Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church (Acts 11:19–26). Paul confronted Peter openly, not behind his back.

Because he stood condemned. Key words. Peter’s conduct was clearly wrong, condemned by his own earlier practice and by the gospel.

For before certain men came from James, he was eating with the Gentiles. Key words. Eating together, perhaps including the Lord’s Supper, was a sign of full fellowship. Peter had learned that God accepts Gentiles (Acts 10:28; 11:3). “Certain men from James”: they may have claimed James’s authority without his approval (Acts 15:24).

But when they came he drew back and separated himself. Key words. Imperfect tense: he gradually withdrew. “Separated” (aphorizō), the same word Pharisees used of themselves (Pharisee means separated one).

Fearing the circumcision party. Key words. Fear of man (Proverbs 29:25), the same weakness that led Peter to deny Jesus.

Where Christians differ: Peter’s authority. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that Peter was the head of the apostles and the first pope, with a primacy passed to his successors, including infallibility in defining doctrine. Verdict: Peter was a great apostle and leader. But here Paul publicly rebukes him for a serious error affecting the gospel. Peter was neither infallible in practice nor above correction by another apostle. The authority of the church rests on the apostolic teaching recorded in Scripture, not on the succession of one office (Ephesians 2:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Peter’s theology was wrong. His practice contradicted his theology. Paul rebukes his hypocrisy.

In a sentence. When Peter came to Antioch, Paul opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself from the Gentiles because he was afraid of those who belonged to the circumcision group.

For worship. Ask God to free you from the fear of what others think, which led even Peter astray.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch in Syria was the first great Gentile church. Eating together was the test: strict Jews would not share a table with Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”

And the rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him. Key words. “Hypocritically” (synypokrinomai, played the actor together). They pretended to believe one thing while acting another. Leaders’ example spreads.

So that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. Key words. Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey, the one who had defended Gentile believers (Acts 11:22–24; 13–14). Even he was swept along.

But when I saw that their conduct was not in step with the truth of the gospel. Key words. “Not in step” (orthopodeō, walking straight, from which orthopaedics). Their behaviour was not walking straight with the gospel. Gospel truth must shape conduct.

I said to Cephas before them all. Key words. Public sin with public effect required public correction (1 Timothy 5:20).

“If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew.” Key words. Peter had been living freely, not keeping Jewish food laws.

“How can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?” Key words. By withdrawing, Peter was effectively telling Gentiles: to have full fellowship with us, you must become Jews. That denied the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul relished confronting Peter. He did it because the gospel was at stake. Later, Peter spoke warmly of Paul (2 Peter 3:15).

In a sentence. The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray. When Paul saw that they were not acting in line with the truth of the gospel, he said to Peter in front of them all, “You are a Jew, yet you live like a Gentile and not like a Jew. How is it, then, that you force Gentiles to follow Jewish customs?”

On a Tuesday. Does your conduct walk in step with the gospel? Do you treat all believers as equally accepted in Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas had been Paul’s partner on the first journey.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul spells out the principle. Even Jewish believers know that no one is justified by doing what the law requires but only through faith in Jesus Christ, so they too have trusted Christ in order to be justified by faith. If seeking justification in Christ shows that we are still sinners, that does not make Christ a servant of sin; rebuilding the law as a way of standing with God is what makes a person a transgressor. Through the law Paul died to the law so that he might live for God. He has been crucified with Christ; his life now is Christ living in him, and he lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him. He will not set aside God’s grace, for if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith: The Article by Which the Church Stands or Falls

Protestant theology came to call justification by faith articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae, the article by which the church stands or falls — a summary of Luther’s own conviction — and vv. 15–21 are the classic passage for it. Justification is forensic — a declaration of status, not an infusion of goodness, though transformation certainly follows. It is by faith alone, its object is Christ alone, and it is by grace alone; and the Reformed tradition has always insisted the three stand or fall together. If faith is not the exclusive instrument, it is not by grace; if Christ is not the exclusive object of faith, it is not grace either.

One point of translation deserves noting since a reader may meet it. The phrase rendered faith in Jesus Christ in v. 16 can also be read as “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ” — his own obedience to the cross as the ground of acceptance. The majority Reformed rendering takes it as faith directed toward him; either way, faith is not a work that earns the verdict but the empty hand that takes it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish believers had every religious advantage and still came the same way as the Gentiles they were now refusing to eat with (v. 15). The argument from the insider to the outsider is conclusive: if the law cannot justify those to whom it was given, it will not justify anyone else. And v. 18 lands directly on Antioch, where stones were going back into a wall that had been pulled down.

Now:The person who comes to faith from a life of moral respectability and the person who comes from obvious wreckage stand on identical ground, with the same righteousness, which is Christ’s. The respectability is as irrelevant to the verdict as the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.

We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners. Key words. Paul continues his words to Peter, perhaps quoting Jewish attitudes. Gentiles were regarded as sinners because they were outside the law.

Yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law. Key words. “Justified” (dikaioō): declared righteous by God the judge, acquitted, accepted. A legal term. “Works of the law”: deeds done in obedience to the law of Moses.

But through faith in Jesus Christ. Key words. Faith receives Christ and his righteousness. The ESV note mentions an alternative: through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ (see below).

So we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law. Key words. Even Jews like Peter and Paul had to give up trusting in law-keeping and trust Christ.

Because by works of the law no one will be justified. Key words. From Psalm 143:2. No human being will be declared righteous by keeping the law, because no one keeps it perfectly (3:10; Romans 3:20).

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? Some scholars of the New Perspective on Paul argue that works of the law mean mainly the boundary markers that separated Jews from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath. So justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people, not how a sinner is made right with God. Verdict: Works of the law certainly include those boundary markers, as the Antioch incident shows. But Paul’s argument goes deeper: no one is justified by the law because no one keeps the whole law (3:10–12; 5:3). Justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, received by faith alone (Romans 4:4–8). It certainly has consequences for who belongs together at the table. But it is first about how a guilty person can stand before a holy God (Westminster 11.1).

What “justified” means, and what it does not. To be justified is to be declared righteous by God as judge: the verdict of not guilty, and more, of accepted as righteous. It is the opposite of being condemned (Romans 8:33–34; Deuteronomy 25:1). It does not mean being made inwardly good, though God does that too, in the separate work of sanctification. It does not mean God pretends we are good when we are not. He declares us righteous because the righteousness of Christ is counted to us, credited to our account (Romans 4:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). Our sins were counted to him at the cross; his obedience is counted to us. The verdict rests on what he has done, not on what we are or do.

Where Christians differ: declared righteous or made righteous? The Roman Catholic Church teaches (Council of Trent, 1547) that justification is a process in which God pours grace into the soul and makes the person inwardly righteous; it grows through the sacraments and good works, can be lost by mortal sin, and is restored by penance. On that view a person is accepted by God as far as he has been made righteous. The Reformers taught that justification is God’s once-for-all legal verdict, received by faith alone, on the ground of Christ’s righteousness alone, and that sanctification, the lifelong work of making us holy, always follows it but is distinct from it. Verdict: The Reformation view is right. Paul’s word is a law-court word: God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5), which cannot mean he finds them already godly. Justification is complete the moment a person believes (Romans 5:1; 8:1), and so it cannot grow or be lost. Works matter greatly, but as the fruit of justification, not its ground (Ephesians 2:8–10; Westminster 11.1–2). If our acceptance depended on how far we had been made righteous, no one could ever be sure of it, and the cross would be only a beginning; but Christ died for no purpose if righteousness comes by anything we do (v. 21).

Where Christians differ: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? The Greek phrase pistis Christou, used twice in this verse, can be read as faith in Christ (our trust in him) or as the faith or faithfulness of Christ (his own faithful obedience to the Father, even to the cross). Some recent scholars prefer the second, and say Paul means we are justified by Christ’s faithfulness. Verdict: Faith in Christ is the better reading. In this very verse Paul adds, “we also have believed in Christ Jesus,” which leaves no doubt that he is talking about our believing. Both truths are biblical: we are saved by Christ’s faithful obedience (Romans 5:19), and we receive it by trusting him. But here Paul’s point is that the way to receive righteousness is believing, not doing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is a work that earns justification. Faith is the empty hand that receives Christ. It is not what we are justified for, but how we receive the one for whose sake we are justified.

In a sentence. We who are Jews by birth and not sinful Gentiles know that a person is not justified by the works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ. So we, too, have put our faith in Christ Jesus that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, because by the works of the law no one will be justified.

For worship. Thank God that you are justified by faith in Christ, not by your record. Rest in that today.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.quote: But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? Certainly not!

But if, in our endeavor to be justified in Christ, we too were found to be sinners. Key words. An objection: by abandoning the law and eating with Gentiles, Jewish believers became, in the eyes of the law, sinners like the Gentiles.

Is Christ then a servant of sin? Key words. Does Christ encourage sin by freeing people from the law? This was the common objection to justification by faith (Romans 6:1).

Certainly not! Key words. Mē genoito. Absolutely not. Christ does not promote sin. Justification by faith leads to holiness, not licence (5:13–25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers do not sin. It means Christ is not to blame for their sin, and the gospel does not encourage it.

In a sentence. But if, in seeking to be justified in Christ, we Jews find ourselves also among the sinners, does that mean Christ promotes sin? Absolutely not!

On a Tuesday. Free grace never means freedom to sin. Live holy because you are free.

verseByVerse.quote: For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God.

For if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself to be a transgressor. Key words. If Paul goes back to the law as a way of righteousness, after tearing it down by trusting Christ, he shows that he was wrong to tear it down, and that he is guilty. Peter, by withdrawing, was rebuilding the wall.

For through the law I died to the law. Key words. The law itself, by condemning him to death, brought him to the end of it. In Christ, who bore the law’s curse, Paul died to the law’s claims (Romans 7:4).

How can the law make me die to the law? This is one of Paul’s most compressed sentences, so it helps to take it in steps. First, the law demands perfect obedience and pronounces death on every transgressor (3:10). Second, Paul was a transgressor, so the law’s sentence on him was death. Third, Christ took that sentence for him: he was “born under the law” (4:4) and died under its curse in his people’s place (3:13). Fourth, Paul was united to Christ by faith, so when Christ died, Paul died with him (v. 20). So the law did carry out its sentence on Paul: in Christ, he died. And a dead man is free from the law’s claim; the law has nothing more to say to someone whose sentence has been fully carried out (Romans 7:1–4, where Paul uses the picture of a marriage ended by death). That is why it was through the law: the law itself demanded the death by which he was set free from it. There is a second strand too: the law, by exposing his sin, drove him to stop trusting it and to flee to Christ (3:24; Romans 7:9–10).

What it does not mean. Dying to the law does not mean becoming lawless. Paul died to the law as a way of being right with God, and as a master that condemns him; he did not die to God’s will. He is now “under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21), and the Spirit leads him to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement in love (5:14; Romans 8:4).

So that I might live to God. Key words. The purpose of dying to the law is not lawlessness but life for God. The law could not make him live for God; Christ does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law is bad or that its moral teaching no longer matters. It means the law is no longer the way to righteousness or the master over believers.
