In a sentence. If Paul rebuilds what he destroyed, then he really would be a lawbreaker. For through the law he died to the law so that he might live for God.

For worship. You died to the law in Christ, so that you might live for God. Live for him today.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.

I have been crucified with Christ. Key words. Perfect tense: crucified, and remain so. United to Christ, Paul shared in his death. His old self, under the law’s condemnation, died (Romans 6:6).

It is no longer I who live. Key words. The old Paul, the self-righteous Pharisee, is gone.

But Christ who lives in me. Key words. Christ now lives in Paul by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Colossians 1:27). Christ is the source and centre of his new life.

And the life I now live in the flesh. Key words. In the body, in this world. Here “the flesh” means ordinary bodily, earthly life, not the sinful nature, which is how Paul uses the word in 5:16–24 and in Romans 8. Paul is saying that his new life in Christ is lived out in a real human body, in the everyday world, by faith.

I live by faith in the Son of God. Key words. Faith is not just the door into the Christian life; it is the way of living it, every day.

Who loved me and gave himself for me. Key words. Personal and particular. Paul does not say only that Christ loved the world, but that he loved me. Christ’s death was a personal act of love for each of his people. Luther said the power of the gospel lies in its pronouns: for me.

What “crucified with Christ” does not mean. It is not a special experience that some advanced Christians reach, nor a feeling to be worked up, nor a command (crucify yourself!). It is a fact that is true of every believer by union with Christ: when he died, we died with him, and that death can never be undone (the perfect tense; Romans 6:3–6). What died was the old self: the person Paul was under the law, condemned and ruled by sin. It does not mean Paul no longer struggles with sin (5:17), or that he no longer has a will of his own. Nor does it mean Paul lost his personality; he is more himself than ever. It means Christ has replaced self as the centre, the source of his life, and the object of his trust. The practical result is in the next words: Paul lives by faith, looking to the Son of God who loved him.

In a sentence. Paul has been crucified with Christ and no longer lives, but Christ lives in him. The life he now lives in the body, he lives by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave himself for him.

For worship. Say it for yourself: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. Then live today by faith in him.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose.

I do not nullify the grace of God. Key words. “Nullify” (atheteō, set aside, reject, cancel). Going back to the law as a way of righteousness cancels grace.

For if righteousness were through the law. Key words. If a right standing with God could be achieved by law-keeping,

Then Christ died for no purpose. Key words. “For no purpose” (dōrean, for nothing, in vain). If we could save ourselves by keeping the law, the cross was unnecessary. Every addition to grace is an insult to the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean obedience is unimportant. It means obedience is not the ground of our acceptance with God.

In a sentence. Paul does not set aside the grace of God, for if righteousness could be gained through the law, Christ died for nothing!

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to earn God’s favour, remember: if you could, Christ died for nothing. Trust his finished work.

3.title: The Promise and the Law: Abraham, Faith, and the Curse
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological heart of Galatians: a sustained argument from Scripture that the gospel of grace by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the foundation on which all of God’s dealings with Abraham and his descendants have always rested. The law came 430 years after the Abrahamic covenant. It cannot therefore revoke the promise made to Abraham; it operates within a different register, serving a different purpose, pointing toward its own fulfillment and supersession in Christ.

Paul opens with an emotional appeal: the Galatians had experienced the Spirit. They knew it. Signs and wonders had accompanied their conversion. Did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? The answer is obvious — and the answer settles the question about the ground of their acceptance with God. The same Spirit-receiving faith that initiated their Christian life is also the ongoing basis of their standing. Maturity in Christ is not a movement from faith toward law; it is a deepening of faith in the one in whom all the law finds its fulfillment.

The chapter’s christological climax is the most audacious claim in the letter: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree’” (v. 13). The cross was not merely a sacrifice; it was a specific legal exchange. Christ took the law’s curse — the curse pronounced on all who fail to keep it perfectly — onto himself, becoming the accused on behalf of the accused, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has finished defending his apostleship and turns on the Galatians themselves, and the first line has no courtesy in it. In v. 1 he calls them un-minded and asks who has bewitched them, when what had been placarded before their eyes was Jesus Christ crucified. Then, instead of an argument, he asks about their own biography. Verse 2 puts the one question he says is sufficient: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? They knew the answer. They were, for the most part, uncircumcised pagans who heard and believed, and God moved in.

Verse 3 exposes the folly precisely: having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Not sin — religion; the whole realm of what a man can do, mark and show. Verse 4 asks whether their suffering was wasted, and then Paul cannot finish the sentence. Verse 5 makes the question present tense: God is still supplying the Spirit and working miracles among them, and the evidence stands in the room while the argument goes on.

The sentence of v. 5 runs on a dash straight into v. 6, so Abraham is not a new topic but the last clause of the question. Genesis 15:6 is quoted: Abraham believed God and it was posted to his account as righteousness. Verse 7 draws the conclusion that overturns the whole Judaizing offer — it is those of faith who are Abraham’s sons. Verse 8 goes further: Scripture pre-gospelled Abraham, so the Gentiles were in view in God’s first sentence to him. And v. 9 sets every believer alongside the patriarch himself: blessed along with Abraham, on the same footing, in one queue.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit Is Received by Faith, and the Reception Settles Everything

The appeal of vv. 2 and 5 is not to religious feeling but to a fact of record: the mechanism by which God gives his Spirit. Reformed theology has always held that the Spirit is the agent of union with Christ and that union with Christ is received by faith alone; here Paul argues it backwards from experience. If the Spirit came through the hearing of the gospel and not through law-works, then the law-works were never the channel, and no later addition can make them one.

The force of v. 3 is that the Christian life is not two-stage. There is no beginning by grace followed by an advance by performance. What justifies also sanctifies, and it is the same Spirit received in the same way from first to last. And vv. 6–9 place this outside the new covenant altogether: Abraham was justified by faith in Genesis 15, two chapters and many years before the sign of circumcision was given in Genesis 17. Justification by faith is not a Christian innovation. It is how God has always dealt with sinners.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were not asking the Galatians to abandon Christ. They were offering completion — take the mark, keep the calendar, and become full sons of Abraham like us. From inside, it looked generous and it looked mature. Paul’s answer in vv. 1–5 is to make them look at their own conversion: nothing in their hands, no circumcision, no Sabbath kept, and God gave them his Spirit. Then vv. 6–9 take Abraham, the Judaizers’ own trump card, and turn it over.

Now: Almost no believer decides to be justified by works; the drift of v. 3 is quieter than that. Over a few years the empty hands fill with real and often good things — a devotional habit, a serving rota, a reputation — and the ground of confidence migrates without anyone noticing the day it moved. The test is the one v. 2 implies. Think of your worst week, and ask whether God was as pleased with you that Sunday as on your best. If something flinches, the flinch is the answer, and vv. 6–9 are the cure: one queue, one way in, and Abraham himself is standing in it.

verseByVerse.quote: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.

Meaning first. Galatians 3 is Paul’s great argument that God has always justified people by faith, not by the law. He argues from their experience: they received the Spirit by believing the gospel, not by keeping the law, so why go back to the flesh now (vv. 1–5)? He argues from Abraham: Abraham believed God and was counted righteous, and God promised that in him all nations would be blessed; so those of faith are Abraham’s true children (vv. 6–9). He argues from the law itself: the law curses everyone who fails to keep it completely, and Scripture says the righteous live by faith; Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us on the cross (vv. 10–14). He argues from history: God’s covenant promise to Abraham and his offspring, Christ, came 430 years before the law and cannot be cancelled by it (vv. 15–18). Then he explains why the law was given: it was added because of transgressions, to imprison all under sin and act as a guardian until Christ came (vv. 19–25). Now, through faith, all believers are God’s children, clothed with Christ, one in him whatever their race, status or sex, and heirs of the promise to Abraham (vv. 26–29).

O foolish Galatians! Key words. “Foolish” (anoētoi, without understanding, senseless). Not stupid, but failing to think clearly about what they know.

Who has bewitched you? Key words. “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye (baskainō). The false teaching was like a spell, fascinating them away from the truth. Galatia was a region full of magic and superstition.

It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified. Key words. “Publicly portrayed” (prographō, placarded, posted up like a public notice). Paul preached Christ crucified so vividly that it was as if they saw it with their own eyes. How could they look away from the cross to the law?

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul literally showed them a picture. It means his preaching set the crucified Christ clearly before them.

In a sentence. You foolish Galatians! Who has cast a spell on you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified.

On a Tuesday. Keep Christ crucified before your eyes. When you are tempted to trust your own performance, look at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: “Bewitched” pictures someone under a spell or the evil eye. “Publicly portrayed” uses the word for a public notice posted for all to read.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?

Let me ask you only this. Key words. One question settles the matter.

Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith? Key words. The Spirit is the mark of belonging to God (Romans 8:9). How did they receive him? Not by keeping the law, but by hearing the gospel and believing it. “Hearing with faith” (akoē pisteōs): either the hearing that is faith, or the message that produces faith (Romans 10:17). Since they began with the Spirit by faith, they do not need the law to be complete.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit is received in a second experience after faith. They received him when they believed.

In a sentence. Paul would like to learn just one thing from you: did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by believing what you heard?

For worship. Thank God that you received the Spirit as a gift, by faith, not by your works.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?

Are you so foolish? Key words. Repeated in amazement.

Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh? Key words. “Perfected” (epiteleō, completed, brought to maturity). The false teachers said: faith is the start, but circumcision and law-keeping complete you. Paul says: you cannot complete by the flesh, by human effort and outward rituals, what the Spirit began. The Christian life is lived the same way it began: by the Spirit, through faith.

Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain? Key words. “Suffer” (paschō), or experience. They had suffered persecution for the gospel (Acts 14:2, 5, 19, 22). Or it may mean experienced so many blessings. Either way, would they throw it away? Paul hopes it is not in vain.

Where Christians differ: sanctification by effort? Some think justification is by faith, but sanctification is by our own effort and rule-keeping. Verdict: Sanctification, like justification, is a work of the Spirit received by faith. It involves real effort and obedience (Philippians 2:12–13), but effort that depends on the Spirit, not on the flesh. Christians grow not by adding laws but by walking in the Spirit (5:16, 25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians make no effort. It means the effort is Spirit-empowered faith, not self-reliant striving.

In a sentence. Are you so foolish? After beginning by means of the Spirit, are you now trying to finish by means of the flesh? Have you experienced so much in vain, if it really was in vain?

On a Tuesday. Are you trying to grow as a Christian by your own willpower? Ask the Spirit to work in you, and walk by faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith— just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?

Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you. Key words. God continues to supply the Spirit and to do miracles among them (Acts 14:3, 8–10).

Do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith? Key words. The same question as verse 2. The answer is obvious: by faith.

Just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.” Key words. From Genesis 15:6. The false teachers appealed to Abraham, who was circumcised (Genesis 17). Paul appeals to Abraham too: before he was circumcised, he was counted righteous by faith (Romans 4:9–11). “Counted” (logizomai, credited, reckoned): God credited righteousness to his account. This is imputation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith itself is the righteousness. Faith is the means by which righteousness, God’s gift in Christ, is received.

In a sentence. So again: does God give you his Spirit and work miracles among you because you keep the law, or because you believe what you heard? So also Abraham “believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”

For worship. Like Abraham, believe God. Trust his promise, and his righteousness is credited to you.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.

Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham. Key words. Abraham’s true children are not his physical descendants or those circumcised, but those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12, 16; John 8:39).

And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith. Key words. Scripture is personified: what Scripture says, God says. God planned from the start to justify Gentiles by faith.

Preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham. Key words. The gospel was announced in advance to Abraham. The gospel is not new; it is the fulfilment of God’s oldest promise.

Saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.” Key words. From Genesis 12:3 and 18:18. God’s plan was always worldwide: blessing for all nations through Abraham.

So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith. Key words. “Man of faith” (pistos, believing, or faithful). Gentile believers share Abraham’s blessing: justification, the Spirit, and the inheritance.

Where Christians differ: Israel and the church. Dispensationalists distinguish sharply between Israel and the church as two peoples with separate promises. Verdict: Paul teaches that all who have faith, Jew or Gentile, are Abraham’s children and heirs of the promise (v. 29). There is one people of God across history, united by faith in the promised offspring, Christ. This is covenant theology’s insight: the one covenant of grace, administered in different ways, runs from Abraham to the church (Westminster 7.5–6). God’s purposes for ethnic Israel continue (Romans 11), but within the one people, not alongside it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Abraham knew all the details of the gospel. He trusted God’s promise, which pointed to Christ (John 8:56).

In a sentence. Understand, then, that those who have faith are children of Abraham. Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and announced the gospel in advance to Abraham: “All nations will be blessed through you.” So those who rely on faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, you are Abraham’s child, whatever your background. Live as an heir of his blessing.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having proved his case from Abraham, Paul now proves it from the law, and he does it by letting the law speak. Verse 10 says something nobody expects: it is not those who break the law who are under a curse but those who rely on it — the serious, observant, early-rising ones. The proof is Deuteronomy 27:26, the last of the twelve curses Israel answered with its own Amen. Four words carry it: everyone, all things, abide by, and do them. The law is not a pass mark; it is a seamless garment, and it cannot be scored out of a hundred.

Verse 11 states the conclusion as something already plain — no one is justified before God by the law — and grounds it in Habakkuk 2:4, the verse that broke the medieval church open. Verse 12 sets the opposing principle beside it from Leviticus 18:5: the one who does them shall live by them. A thoughtful reader feels the difficulty, since Leviticus is God’s word too. The answer is that the law’s offer was never a bluff; the fault lies not in the law but in the material it works with.

Then v. 13, the summit of the chapter. Christ redeemed us — bought us out of the slave market — from the law’s curse by becoming a curse himself, and the text quoted is Deuteronomy 21:23, the very verse that made a crucified Messiah unthinkable to Saul the Pharisee. Verse 14 gives the purpose twice: so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith — which closes the circle opened by the question in v. 2.
verseByVerse.theology:
Penal Substitution: The Curse Exchanged

That Christ bore the penalty due to sinners in their place, exhausting the law’s sentence, is not a later development of doctrine but the explicit content of v. 13. The exchange is legally precise. The curse of vv. 10–12 fell on him, so that the blessing of v. 14 could fall on those who have no claim to it. This is not sympathetic solidarity — he suffered with us — but substitution: he suffered instead of us, bearing what was ours.

Two guards belong here. First, becoming a curse does not mean the Father ceased to love the Son or turned on him in temper; Jesus said the opposite (John 10:17). The sentence was real and the Father’s delight in the obedient Son was real at the same hour. Second, the Deuteronomy text is about the public display of an already-condemned man, so the tree did not make him cursed — it published the verdict. Saul had read that publication correctly and been wrong about only one thing: whose curse it was.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers offered the law as a supplement, a way of securing what faith had begun. Verses 10–12 show that the law has no supplementary setting. It accepts one condition only, and no son of Adam has ever met it, so those who take their stand there have entered a system whose only two verdicts are flawless obedience and curse. Verse 13 names the single exit, and vv. 13–14 together explain how a Gentile with no covenant and no ancestry ends up holding the Spirit of God.

Now: Some readers come to v. 10 with their stomach already tight, half expecting confirmation that God is disappointed with them. Read it exactly. The curse is aimed not at their failure but at the thing they were using to cover it. And v. 13 says what became of it: the sentence was carried out, and not on you. Verse 14 adds that the Spirit you already have is the receipt.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”

For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse. Key words. “Rely on” is literally are of the works of the law: those whose standing with God depends on law-keeping. The law offers blessing for obedience and curse for disobedience. Since no one obeys perfectly, all who rely on it are under its curse.

For it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.” Key words. From Deuteronomy 27:26. Everyone. All things. The law demands perfect, complete obedience. One failure brings the curse (James 2:10). The unstated premise: no one does all things.

What it does not mean. It does not mean obeying the law is bad. It means no sinner can obey it perfectly, so it cannot be the way to blessing.

In a sentence. For all who rely on the works of the law are under a curse, as it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.”

For worship. Thank God that you do not have to stand on your own record. Christ has taken the curse.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.” But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”

Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law. Key words. Before God: in his sight, by his standard.

For “The righteous shall live by faith.” Key words. From Habakkuk 2:4 (also Romans 1:17; Hebrews 10:38). The way to life is by faith. The verse that sparked Luther’s understanding of the gospel.

But the law is not of faith. Key words. As a way to righteousness, the law works on a different principle from faith.

Rather “The one who does them shall live by them.” Key words. From Leviticus 18:5. The law’s principle is: do and live. Faith’s principle is: believe and live. They are opposite ways. Since no one does them perfectly, life by the law is impossible.

How can Paul set Moses against Habakkuk? It can look as if Paul is pitting one Old Testament verse against another. He is not. In Leviticus 18:5, God speaks to a people he has already redeemed from Egypt: keep my laws and you will enjoy life with me in the land. For them, obedience was the grateful way of life of the redeemed, and the sacrifices were provided for their failures. But the false teachers were using the law as a ladder to climb up to God: do these things and you will be accepted. Paul takes them at their word. If you make the law the ground of your acceptance, then Leviticus 18:5 states the terms: you must do them, all of them (v. 10), to live by them. No sinner can meet those terms. Habakkuk 2:4 states the other way, the only way open to sinners: the righteous live by trusting God. Christ is the one person who met the terms of Leviticus 18:5, and he did it for us (4:4–5; Romans 10:4–5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law was never connected with faith. Old Testament believers lived by faith too. It means the law as a system of earning life is opposed to faith.

In a sentence. Clearly no one who relies on the law is justified before God, because “the righteous will live by faith.” The law is not based on faith; on the contrary, it says, “The person who does these things will live by them.”

On a Tuesday. Live by faith today, not by trying to prove yourself.

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith
by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law. Key words. “Redeemed” (exagorazō, bought out, as a slave is bought out of the market). The curse is the penalty the law pronounces on lawbreakers: death and God’s wrath.

By becoming a curse for us. Key words. “For us” (hyper hēmōn, on our behalf, in our place). Christ took the curse we deserved. This is penal substitution: he bore the penalty, so that we are free.

For it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.” Key words. Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was a sign that he was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23). To Jews, a crucified Messiah was unthinkable for this reason (1 Corinthians 1:23). Paul sees it as the very point: Christ was cursed for us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ was personally guilty or that God stopped loving his Son. He bore our curse as our substitute, in perfect obedience and love.

In a sentence. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written: “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a pole.”

For worship. Christ became a curse for you. Look at the cross and thank him.
verseByVerse.note: Under the law, the body of an executed criminal hung on a tree was under God’s curse.

parallels.desc: a hanged man is cursed by God

verseByVerse.quote: so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.

So that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles. Key words. The purpose of the cross: the blessing promised to Abraham, justification and life, now flows to the nations (v. 8).

So that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith. Key words. The Spirit was promised by the prophets (Joel 2:28; Ezekiel 36:27). He is received through faith, not law-keeping (v. 2). The blessing of Abraham and the gift of the Spirit go together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews are excluded. “We” includes Jewish and Gentile believers.

In a sentence. He redeemed us in order that the blessing given to Abraham might come to the Gentiles through Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. You have the Spirit by faith. Depend on him today.

parallels.desc: I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temperature drops and Paul takes the Galatians from Golgotha to a lawyer’s office, calling them brothers again, a warm word breaking through the anger. Verse 15 gives the principle from everyday life: once a covenant or will has been ratified, no one annuls it or adds a clause. If that holds for a document drawn up by men who forget things and change their minds, how much more for one God has sworn. The Judaizers were not proposing to tear up the promise; they were proposing an amendment, and an amendment is not a modest adjustment but a legal impossibility.

Verse 16 makes the exegetical observation that troubles modern readers: the promise was made to Abraham’s offspring, singular, who is Christ. Since the word is collective in both Hebrew and Greek, this looks like a trick — until you notice that Paul himself uses it collectively in v. 29. The argument is not about grammar in isolation but about the shape of the history. The promise narrowed at every fork: Isaac not Ishmael, Jacob not Esau, Judah, David. It was always funnelling toward one person.

Verse 17 dates it. The law came 430 years after the promise, and the later document cannot cancel the earlier one; the figure follows the Greek Old Testament Paul’s churches used, which counts from Abraham to the exodus. Verse 18 states the either-or underneath: if the inheritance comes by law it no longer comes by promise. These are not two ingredients that improve each other but two answers to the question of who is responsible for my standing, and the second cancels the first.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Priority and Indestructibility of the Promise

The covenant of grace — God’s unconditional oath to bless all nations through Abraham’s seed — is prior to the Mosaic law and independent of it. This is a foundation of Reformed covenant theology, and vv. 15 and 17 are where Paul argues it. The Mosaic administration does not replace the Abrahamic covenant or amend its terms; it operates within it and serves it for a season, leaving its character as promise untouched.

Verse 16 supplies the reason the promise cannot fail, and it is more than a point of grammar. Had God covenanted with Abraham’s descendants as a body, the covenant would have rested in the hands of a nation that broke every arrangement it was given. He covenanted with one heir who would not break it, and everyone else inherits by being in him. Verse 18 draws the practical edge: God “has given” it, in the perfect tense, and it stands given. A promise whose security is the character of the one who swore it is a different kind of possession from anything conditioned on the one who receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers were arguing, in effect, that the later Mosaic legislation modified the conditions of the earlier Abrahamic promise. Verses 15 and 17 show why that is not a theological preference but a legal impossibility, and v. 18 shows what it would cost if it were allowed: not an improved promise but no promise at all. Verse 16 removes their last foothold by identifying the heir they were claiming to represent.

Now: The difference v. 18 describes is invisible from the outside. Two Christians can keep the same hours, give the same money and serve on the same rota, one obeying a Father who has already given him the house, the other trying to secure a house he is not sure of. You can tell them apart only when something goes wrong: one fails and runs to his Father, the other fails and hides, because for him the failure has moved the inheritance. Verses 15–18 exist to put every reader in the first category and keep him there.

verseByVerse.quote: To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.

To give a human example, brothers. Key words. An illustration from everyday life.

Even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified. Key words. “Covenant” (diathēkē) can also mean a will or testament. Once a will is signed and legally confirmed, no one can change it. How much more God’s covenant.

Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. Key words. God’s promises to Abraham (Genesis 12:7; 13:15; 17:8; 22:18).

It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ. Key words. “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one person or many. Paul knows it often means many descendants (he uses it that way in v. 29). But the promise ultimately focuses on one descendant: the Messiah, through whom the blessing comes. All the promises find their fulfilment in Christ, and those united to him share in them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is playing with grammar. He sees that Scripture narrows the promise from Abraham’s many descendants to the line of Isaac, of Judah, of David, and finally to Christ.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, let Paul take an example from everyday life. Just as no one can set aside or add to a human covenant that has been duly established, so it is in this case. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Scripture does not say “and to seeds,” meaning many people, but “and to your seed,” meaning one person, who is Christ.

For worship. Every promise of God to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ, and through him, to you. Praise God for his faithfulness.
verseByVerse.note: “Offspring” (literally “seed”) is a singular noun that can refer to one descendant or many.

parallels.desc: in your offspring shall all the nations be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.

This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward. Key words. Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt (Exodus 12:40); Paul uses this figure for the gap between the promise to Abraham and the law at Sinai, counting from the promises to the patriarchs. The law came long after the promise.

Does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void. Key words. A later law cannot cancel an earlier promise. God’s covenant with Abraham stands.

For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise. Key words. Inheritance and law are opposite principles. An inheritance is given; a wage is earned.

But God gave it to Abraham by a promise. Key words. “Gave” (charizomai, gave freely, as a gift of grace). Perfect tense: given once and permanently. Salvation is a promise received, not a reward earned.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law was pointless. Paul explains its purpose next.

In a sentence. What Paul means is this: the law, introduced 430 years later, does not set aside the covenant previously established by God and thus do away with the promise. For if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on the promise; but God in his grace gave it to Abraham through a promise.

On a Tuesday. Your inheritance in Christ rests on God’s promise, not your performance. Rest in it.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus gives 430 years for Israel’s stay in Egypt; Paul uses the figure for the long gap between the promise and the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–25 — The Purpose of the Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If the law cannot justify, cannot give life and cannot amend the promise, the obvious objection has to be faced, and v. 19 faces it: why then the law? Paul answers with three phrases, each of which puts the law in its place without insulting it. It was added because of transgressions — drawing the line that turns vague wrongness into named counts. It was until the offspring should come, with an expiry written into it, not a failure but a term. And it was put in place through angels by an intermediary, which is the sharpest demotion of all.

Verse 20 is the most compressed sentence in the letter, and honest commentators admit that its details are disputed. But the direction is clear from the chain Paul has just counted. A mediator implies two parties; the presence of Moses on the mountain tells you Sinai was a two-sided arrangement that could fail, and it failed at the foot of the mountain. God is one: when he came to Abraham there was no second party, and in Genesis 15 he passed alone between the pieces while Abraham slept through his own covenant.

Verse 21 asks whether the law is therefore contrary to God’s promises and answers with Paul’s strongest negative. They are not rivals but a diagnosis and a cure. He grants freely that if any law could give life, righteousness would have come that way. Verse 22 gives the true verdict: Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, shut in like fish in a net, so that the promise might be given by faith. Verses 23–25 name the jailer’s office — the law was our paidagōgos, the household slave who walked the boy to school until he came of age. Verse 24 says he was doing it so we might be justified by faith, and v. 25 says the arrangement has ended.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Law as Guardian: Genuine, Severe, Temporary, Fulfilled

Reformed theology has always held to the unity of the covenant of grace across both Testaments while recognising the distinct function of the Mosaic administration within it. Verses 19 and 24 are the classic ground for that. The law was genuinely from God, genuinely binding in its time, and genuinely serving the covenant of grace — but it was designed for a phase and not for the end. Its close as a system of justification is not God changing his mind; it is God completing his plan.

Two guards belong with vv. 23–25. It does not follow that God’s moral will has been repealed: Paul will say in 5:14 that the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour. What has ended is the law as the framework of the relationship, the guardianship under which the people of God lived as minors. Nor does it follow that Old Testament believers were second-class. They were children in the same family under the care their age required. And v. 22 shows the severity was mercy: the exits were closed so that the one open door would finally be taken.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted the guardian reinstated after the child had come of age. Verse 19 answers that the guardian was appointed for a term that has expired, v. 20 that the promise never depended on two signatures anyway, and v. 25 that the arrangement is over.

Now: Verses 21–25 meet three readers: the one who assumes his problem is information or willpower, the one who finds that the harder he tries the worse the accounting gets, and the largest group of all — believers who are adults in Christ and still live as if under supervision.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.

Why then the law? Key words. The obvious question. If the law does not save, why did God give it?

It was added because of transgressions. Key words. To reveal sin as transgression, deliberate breaking of God’s known law (Romans 3:20; 4:15; 5:20); and to restrain sin. The law makes sin visible and shows our need of a Saviour.

Until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made. Key words. The law was temporary, until Christ. Its role as the governing covenant ended when he came.

And it was put in place through angels. Key words. Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law (Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek; Acts 7:53; Hebrews 2:2).

By an intermediary. Key words. Moses, who stood between God and the people (Deuteronomy 5:5). The law came indirectly, while the promise came directly from God.

Where Christians differ: the uses of the law. Some say the law has no role for Christians at all; others make it the centre of the Christian life. Verdict: The Reformers identified three uses of the law. First, it shows sin and drives sinners to Christ (the use Paul focuses on here). Second, it restrains evil in society. Third, it guides believers in how to please God, as the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments (Romans 13:8–10). The ceremonial and civil laws of Israel were fulfilled and ended in Christ, but the moral law remains the rule of life, not as a covenant of works, but as the will of our Father (Westminster 19.5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law is evil or that God changed his mind. It was always meant to point to Christ.

In a sentence. Why, then, was the law given at all? It was added because of transgressions until the Seed to whom the promise referred had come. The law was given through angels and entrusted to a mediator.

For worship. Thank God for his law, which showed you your sin and sent you to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the law; Moses was the intermediary.

parallels.desc: I stood between the LORD and you

verseByVerse.quote: Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.

Now an intermediary implies more than one. Key words. A mediator stands between two parties, each with obligations. The law at Sinai was a covenant with conditions on both sides, through Moses.

But God is one. Key words. The promise to Abraham was God’s alone, unconditional, depending only on him. In Genesis 15, God alone passed between the pieces of the sacrifice, binding only himself. One of the most difficult verses in Paul; there are reportedly hundreds of interpretations. But the main point is clear: the promise is greater than the law because it rests on God alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is not a mediator. Christ is the one mediator between God and man (1 Timothy 2:5), and he is himself God.

In a sentence. A mediator, however, implies more than one party; but God is one.

On a Tuesday. Your salvation rests on God alone, not on your side of a bargain. Trust him.

verseByVerse.quote: Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.

Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! Key words. The law and the promise are not enemies. They serve different purposes in God’s one plan.

For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law. Key words. The law cannot give life. It can command but not empower; it can show the way but not carry us along it (Romans 8:3).

But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin. Key words. “Imprisoned” (synkleiō, shut up together, locked in). Scripture declares all people guilty, locked in a prison with no escape (Romans 3:9–20; 11:32).

So that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. Key words. The purpose of the prison: to make us look for the only way out, the promise received by faith in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is cruel. He shuts us up in order to set us free.

In a sentence. Is the law, therefore, opposed to the promises of God? Absolutely not! For if a law had been given that could impart life, then righteousness would certainly have come by the law. But Scripture has locked up everything under the control of sin, so that what was promised, being given through faith in Jesus Christ, might be given to those who believe.

For worship. Thank God that he locked you in by the law, so that he could set you free in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith. But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,

Now before faith came. Key words. Before the coming of Christ and the gospel age of faith. Not that no one had faith before, but that the age of faith in its fullness began with Christ.

We were held captive under the law. Key words. “Held captive” (phroureō, guarded, kept under watch). Israel was guarded by the law.

Imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed. Key words. A temporary custody.

So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came. Key words. The “guardian” (paidagōgos) was a household slave who supervised a boy until he came of age: taking him to school, disciplining him, protecting him. Not the teacher, but the supervisor. The law guarded and disciplined Israel until Christ.

In order that we might be justified by faith. Key words. The law’s purpose was to lead to justification by faith in Christ.

But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian. Key words. Christ has come. The child has come of age. The guardian’s job is done.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers may live as they please. Grown sons still honour their father’s will, but from love, not as children under supervision.

In a sentence. Before the coming of this faith, we were held in custody under the law, locked up until the faith that was to come would be revealed. So the law was our guardian until Christ came that we might be justified by faith. Now that this faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.

On a Tuesday. You are no longer a child under a guardian. Live as a grown son or daughter of God, from love and freedom.
verseByVerse.note: The “guardian” (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised a child, took him to school and kept him in line until he came of age.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Through faith, all of them are sons of God in Christ Jesus, for all who were baptised into Christ have put him on like a garment. In him the divisions that ruled the ancient world, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, no longer determine anyone’s standing; all are one in Christ. And if they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring and heirs of the promise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ, and the Unity It Creates

Verses 26–27 give the ground of everything Paul has argued: the believer’s standing is not a quality in himself but a location. He is in Christ, clothed in Christ, and therefore holds the status of the Son. This is why assurance is possible for people who know themselves well; the clothing does not fluctuate with the wearer.

Verse 28 is the theological ground of the New Testament’s social revolution. The gospel does not merely change individuals, it creates a community in which the stratifications of the old age no longer determine worth or access. Sincere believers who honour this book read the verse differently when it comes to office and order, some hearing the end of every distinction of role, others holding that Paul speaks of standing here and of roles elsewhere, which is the more natural reading of the whole Pauline corpus. What neither side qualifies is what the verse indisputably says, and it is the larger thing: at the cross there is no hierarchy of worth, and in the inheritance of v. 29 there is no smaller share.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jew and Greek was a divide so absolute that a Jew would not enter a Gentile house; slave and free described perhaps a third of a city’s population as property; male and female determined whose testimony counted in court. A saying recorded in later rabbinic sources thanked God for not having been made a Gentile, a slave, or a woman. Verse 28 takes those three walls and says they do not run through the room. Verses 26–27 explain why: everyone in it is wearing the same garment. Verse 29 tells Gentile believers they are not associate members of a Jewish covenant but full heirs.

Now:Every congregation holds people who have quietly concluded they are second rank. Verse 28 does not offer them a role; it says something better and harder to believe, that Christ has no larger portion for anyone in the building.

verseByVerse.quote: for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith. Key words. Not just children under a guardian, but adult sons with full rights of inheritance (4:5–7). “Sons” includes daughters; in that culture, sons were the heirs, and Paul gives all believers that status. In Christ: by union with him. Through faith: the means.

For as many of you as were baptized into Christ. Key words. Paul’s readers had been baptised in water when they believed, and he speaks of their baptism as the moment they were joined to Christ, because in the New Testament faith and baptism belonged together: people believed and were baptised at once (Acts 8:12; 16:31–33). Baptism is the visible sign of that union (Romans 6:3–4). What actually unites a person to Christ is the Spirit, received through faith (v. 14; 1 Corinthians 12:13); water baptism is the outward picture and public confession of it. So Paul can speak of the sign and mean the reality it signifies, as we might say “she gave her hand in marriage” and mean the whole covenant of marriage.

Have put on Christ. Key words. “Put on” (endyō, clothe oneself). Like putting on a garment. In Rome, a boy coming of age put on the toga of manhood. Believers have put on Christ: covered with his righteousness, identified with him.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some take this verse to mean that water baptism itself unites a person to Christ and regenerates them. Verdict: Paul has just said we are sons through faith (v. 26). Baptism is the sign and seal of union with Christ, which is received by faith. It is not the cause of union. Those who are baptised with faith truly put on Christ; baptism without faith does not save (1 Peter 3:21; Westminster 28.5; London Baptist Confession 29.1). This app holds believer’s baptism: the sign follows the faith it signifies, which is exactly the order in this verse: sons through faith (v. 26), then baptised into Christ (v. 27).

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism is unimportant. It is commanded and precious. But it is not magic.

In a sentence. So in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith, for all of you who were baptised into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.

For worship. You are clothed with Christ. Thank God for your new garment.

verseByVerse.quote: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

There is neither Jew nor Greek. Key words. The great ethnic divide. In Christ, no advantage or disadvantage.

There is neither slave nor free. Key words. The great social divide.

There is no male and female. Key words. The gender divide. The wording echoes Genesis 1:27: male and female he created them. A Jewish man’s morning prayer reportedly thanked God that he was not made a Gentile, a slave or a woman. Paul reverses all three.

For you are all one in Christ Jesus. Key words. One (heis, one person). All believers stand equally in Christ: equally justified, equally sons, equally heirs.

Where Christians differ: does this verse abolish gender roles? Egalitarians use this verse to argue that all distinctions of role between men and women in the church and home are abolished in Christ. Verdict: The context is about who is justified and who is an heir of Abraham: all believers equally, regardless of race, class or sex. It is about status before God, not roles in the church. The distinctions themselves are not abolished: Jews remain Jews, men remain men. Paul elsewhere teaches distinct roles for men and women in the home and church (1 Corinthians 11:3; Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Timothy 2:12), grounded in creation. Equal in worth, distinct in calling: the complementarian view.

What it does not mean. It does not mean differences of ethnicity, status or sex are unimportant in life. It means they do not affect our standing with God.

In a sentence. There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Look at the people in your church who are different from you. In Christ, you are one. Treat them so.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

And if you are Christ’s. Key words. If you belong to Christ, the one offspring (v. 16).

Then you are Abraham’s offspring. Key words. Now Paul uses offspring in its collective sense. In Christ, all believers are Abraham’s seed.

Heirs according to promise. Key words. Heirs of everything God promised Abraham: righteousness, the Spirit, the world to come (Romans 4:13). Not by law, but by promise. The argument of the chapter comes to its conclusion: the Gentile Galatians do not need circumcision to become Abraham’s children. They already are, in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ethnic Israel has no further place in God’s plan. It means every believer, Jew or Gentile, is a full heir.

In a sentence. If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.

For worship. You are an heir of God’s promises to Abraham. Thank him for your inheritance in Christ.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? It was before your eyes that Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.<sup>2</sup>Let me ask you only this: Did you receive the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith?<sup>3</sup>Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?<sup>4</sup>Did you suffer so many things in vain—if indeed it was in vain?<sup>5</sup>Does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the law, or by hearing with faith—<sup>6</sup>just as Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”?<sup>7</sup>Know then that it is those of faith who are the sons of Abraham.<sup>8</sup>And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”<sup>9</sup>So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.<sup>10</sup>For all who rely on works of the law are under a curse; for it is written, “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”<sup>11</sup>Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law, for “The righteous shall live by faith.”<sup>12</sup>But the law is not of faith, rather “The one who does them shall live by them.”<sup>13</sup>Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us—for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”—<sup>14</sup>so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.<sup>15</sup>To give a human example, brothers: even with a man-made covenant, no one annuls it or adds to it once it has been ratified.<sup>16</sup>Now the promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring. It does not say, “And to offsprings,” referring to many, but referring to one, “And to your offspring,” who is Christ.<sup>17</sup>This is what I mean: the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to make the promise void.<sup>18</sup>For if the inheritance comes by the law, it no longer comes by promise; but God gave it to Abraham by a promise.<sup>19</sup>Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, and it was put in place through angels by an intermediary.<sup>20</sup>Now an intermediary implies more than one, but God is one.<sup>21</sup>Is the law then contrary to the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would indeed be by the law.<sup>22</sup>But the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe.<sup>23</sup>Now before faith came, we were held captive under the law, imprisoned until the coming faith would be revealed.<sup>24</sup>So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.<sup>25</sup>But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian,<sup>26</sup>for in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God, through faith.<sup>27</sup>For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.<sup>28</sup>There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.<sup>29</sup>And if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise.

4.title: Sons and Heirs: From Slavery to Sonship
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the emotional and theological apex of the letter’s central argument. Paul has shown that the law functions as a guardian for children; now he shows what the alternative is: full sonship, the Spirit of the Son, and the cry of “Abba! Father!” from the depths of the adopted heart. The contrast is not merely between two systems but between two existences — the existence of the slave who must perform, and the existence of the son who simply belongs.

The chapter’s opening argument (vv. 1–7) draws on the legal reality of an heir who is underage: he possesses everything but controls nothing, lives under guardians and managers until the time set by the father. Israel under the law was in this condition — heirs of the promise but living under the law’s custody until “the fullness of time.” Then God acted: he sent his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. And confirmation: he sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who cries “Abba! Father!” — the most intimate address to God in all of Scripture, the word Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), now placed on the lips of every adopted child of God.

The chapter then turns to a personal appeal (vv. 12–20) of remarkable emotional intensity — Paul reminding the Galatians of how they received him when he first came to them, sick and in need, and how they would have plucked out their eyes for him. His anguish over their drift is the anguish of a parent whose children are being led away: “for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!” Finally, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah (vv. 21–31) makes the theological point in narrative form: the two covenants produce two kinds of children, and only the children of the free woman — the children of promise, of grace, of the Spirit — are the true heirs of the heavenly Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul illustrates with an heir who is still a child: though he owns the estate, he is no better off than a slave, living under guardians until the time his father has set. In the same way, we were enslaved to the basic principles of this world. But when the appointed time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman and born under the law, to redeem those under the law so that we might be adopted as sons. And because they are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying out “Abba! Father!” So they are no longer slaves but sons, and heirs through God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adoption, and the Double Sending of Son and Spirit

Verses 4–6 are among the most trinitarian sentences Paul ever wrote. The Father sends the Son; the Father sends the Spirit of the Son. The two missions are distinct and inseparable: the Son accomplishes redemption and adoption as objective legal realities outside us, and the Spirit applies them within, so that the adopted child knows the Father and calls him by name.

Adoption (huiothesia) is the doctrine this chapter states most clearly, and it goes beyond forgiveness. In Roman practice the adopted son took the father’s name, inherited on the same footing as any natural son, and, in some forms of Roman adoption, found his former obligations extinguished; the act was witnessed and irreversible, because what had changed was not his conduct but his family. Verse 7 draws the conclusion in three words — no longer, son, heir — and adds through God, so that nobody imagines an inheritance of this size arriving any other way. J. I. Packer called adoption the highest privilege the gospel offers.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians already had everything vv. 4–7 describe. They had the Spirit, they had cried Abba, they were heirs. The Judaizers were offering them a route to a standing they already held, and Paul’s answer in vv. 1–3 is to show them what they would be going back to: the nursery, the guardians, the managers, and a calendar. A son does not earn his way into a family he is already in.

Now:The test v. 3 suggests catches good practices rather than bad ones, and v. 6 answers the reader who does not feel like a son: the Spirit is sent because you are one, so the feeling is the consequence of the status and never the cause of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything, but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.

Meaning first. Galatians 4 continues the argument that believers are God’s free sons, not slaves under the law. First, Paul uses the picture of an heir who, while a child, is no better off than a slave, until the time his father set. So humanity was enslaved under elementary principles until the fullness of time, when God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law and give them adoption. Because they are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, crying Abba, Father (vv. 1–7). Second, Paul asks how the Galatians, now known by God, can turn back to slavery by observing special days and seasons (vv. 8–11). Third, he makes a tender personal appeal: remember how you welcomed me when I was ill, as if I were Christ himself; I am in the pains of childbirth again until Christ is formed in you (vv. 12–20). Finally, he reads the story of Abraham’s two sons as a picture of two covenants: Hagar and Ishmael, slavery under Sinai; Sarah and Isaac, freedom by promise. Believers are children of the free woman, the Jerusalem above (vv. 21–31).

I mean that the heir, as long as he is a child. Key words. Child (nēpios, infant, minor): a son not yet of legal age.

Is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything. Key words. By right, he owns the estate. In practice, he has no more freedom than a slave.

But he is under guardians and managers. Key words. Guardians (epitropoi) cared for the child; managers (oikonomoi) administered his property.

Until the date set by his father. Key words. In Roman law, the father could set the age of maturity. God set the time for his people’s coming of age: the coming of Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Old Testament believers were unsaved. They were heirs, but in a time of restriction and preparation.

In a sentence. What Paul is saying is that as long as an heir is under age, he is no different from a slave, although he owns the whole estate. He is subject to guardians and trustees until the time set by his father.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, you are no longer a minor under supervision. You have come of age. Live like it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way we also, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world.

In the same way we also, when we were children. Key words. “We”: both Jews and Gentiles before Christ.

Were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world. Key words. The “elementary principles” (stoicheia) may mean the basic rules of religion, both Jewish law and pagan rituals, or the spiritual powers believed to rule the elements and heavenly bodies (Colossians 2:8, 20). The word originally meant elements, like the letters of the alphabet or the basic components of the world. Either way: before Christ, all humanity was in bondage to a religion of rules and powers, unable to set itself free.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law of Moses and paganism are the same. But as ways of approaching God apart from Christ, both enslave.

In a sentence. So also, when we were under age, we were in slavery under the elemental spiritual forces of the world.

For worship. Thank God that you are no longer a slave to empty rituals or dark powers. Christ has set you free.
verseByVerse.note: The “elementary principles” may mean the basic rules of religion, or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

But when the fullness of time had come. Key words. The moment God had set (v. 2). History had been prepared: the Roman peace and roads, the Greek language, the Jewish Scriptures and synagogues across the world, and deep spiritual hunger. Christ came at exactly the right time (Mark 1:15; Ephesians 1:10).

God sent forth his Son. Key words. “Sent forth” (exapostellō): from heaven. The Son existed before he was sent: his pre-existence and deity.

Born of woman. Key words. Truly human, born like any human. Paul does not explicitly mention the virgin birth here, but his wording fits it: born of a woman, with no human father named.

Born under the law. Key words. A Jew, circumcised, obedient to the law of Moses (Luke 2:21–24). He lived under the law and kept it perfectly for us.

To redeem those who were under the law. Key words. “Redeem” (exagorazō, buy out, as in 3:13). He bore the curse of the law to set its prisoners free.

So that we might receive adoption as sons. Key words. “Adoption” (huiothesia, placing as a son). A Roman legal term: an adopted son received full rights as heir. Believers are not just freed slaves but adopted sons. Adoption is a distinct blessing from justification: we are not only declared righteous but welcomed into God’s family (Westminster 12.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ became God’s Son at his birth. He was eternally the Son; he was sent as the Son.

In a sentence. But when the set time had fully come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive adoption to sonship.

For worship. At just the right time, God sent his Son for you. Praise him for the incarnation, and for adopting you.

verseByVerse.quote: And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.

And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts. Key words. God sent his Son (v. 4) and then the Spirit of his Son. Notice the Trinity: Father, Son and Spirit. The Spirit is the Spirit of the Son: he makes us share the Son’s relationship with the Father.

Crying, “Abba! Father!” Key words. “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family, warm and intimate, though not childish. Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). The Spirit enables believers to call God Father with the same confidence (Romans 8:15–16). “Crying” (krazō): a loud, heartfelt cry.

So you are no longer a slave, but a son. Key words. Singular: each believer personally.

And if a son, then an heir through God. Key words. Sons inherit. Believers are heirs of God (Romans 8:17). Through God: by his grace, not by law.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is our Father in the same way he is Christ’s. Christ is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption and grace. But in Christ, we share his place.

In a sentence. Because you are his sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, the Spirit who calls out, “Abba, Father.” So you are no longer a slave, but God’s child; and since you are his child, God has made you also an heir.

On a Tuesday. Pray today with the confidence of a child: Abba, Father.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used within the family.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before they knew God, the Galatians were enslaved to beings that are not really gods. Now that they know God, or rather are known by him, how can they turn back to those weak and worthless principles and want to be enslaved again, observing special days and seasons? Paul fears his labour among them was wasted. He pleads with them to become like him, as he became like them. He recalls how they welcomed him when he first preached to them because of a bodily illness, treating him like an angel of God, even like Christ, and would have torn out their eyes for him. Has he become their enemy by telling the truth? The rivals court them for selfish ends. Paul, like a mother in labour again until Christ is formed in them, wishes he could be with them, because he is at a loss about them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Symmetry of Bondage, and the Goal of Ministry

Paul’s equation in vv. 8–10 of Judaizing observance with the pagan calendar the Galatians had left is about function, not moral equivalence: any God-given thing made the ground of acceptance will behave like an idol. Reformed theology has always held that moralism is not a minor error but a rival gospel that produces its own bondage.

Verse 9 also contains one of Paul’s clearest incidental statements of election, dropped in as a pastoral correction rather than a seminar topic. To be known by God is not for God to learn facts but for God to set his love on a person and claim him (Jer. 1:5). And v. 19 supplies the only metric for ministry the New Testament finally accepts: not attendance, giving or doctrinal precision, but Christ formed — morphōthē, taking shape from within, the word used of a child forming in the womb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians had loved Paul extravagantly in vv. 14–15 and had cooled by v. 16, and vv. 17–18 explain the mechanism. The Judaizers courted them, flattered them, and held the door a few inches short of open. Verse 20 shows what Paul wanted instead: not their allegiance to him but Christ formed in them, which is why he would rather have been in the room than winning on paper.

Now:Verse 10 raises the question every honest reader asks about Christmas, Easter and Sunday, and Paul answers it himself in Romans 14:5–6: what he attacks here is not the observance but the ground. Verses 17–18 describe spiritual manipulation with uncomfortable accuracy, and v. 13 belongs to the reader whose life has been rerouted by his body.

verseByVerse.quote: Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?

Formerly, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those that by nature are not gods. Key words. The Galatians had been pagans, serving idols, which are not truly gods (1 Corinthians 8:4–5).

But now that you have come to know God. Key words. Through the gospel.

Or rather to be known by God. Key words. Paul corrects himself. The deeper truth is not that they found God, but that God knew them, set his love on them (1 Corinthians 8:3; 2 Timothy 2:19). Salvation begins with God’s initiative.

How can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world. Key words. “Weak” (asthenēs) and “worthless” (ptōchos, beggarly, poor). Going back to the law as a system of righteousness is as much slavery as going back to idols. Both are religion without Christ.

Whose slaves you want to be once more? Key words. Why would freed slaves want to go back?

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law of Moses is the same as idolatry. But relying on it instead of Christ is a similar slavery.

In a sentence. Formerly, when you did not know God, you were slaves to those who by nature are not gods. But now that you know God, or rather are known by God, how is it that you are turning back to those weak and miserable forces? Do you wish to be enslaved by them all over again?

For worship. You are known by God. Thank him that he found you, and refuse to go back to slavery.

parallels.desc: no gods, but the work of men’s hands

verseByVerse.quote: You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You observe days and months and seasons and years! I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain.

You observe days and months and seasons and years! Key words. Jewish Sabbaths, new moons, festivals and sabbatical years (Colossians 2:16). The Galatians were adopting the Jewish calendar as a requirement for righteousness. “Observe” (paratēreō, watch scrupulously).

I am afraid I may have labored over you in vain. Key words. Paul fears his work among them was wasted, if they return to slavery.

Where Christians differ: holy days. Some say this verse forbids Christians from keeping any special days, including Sunday or Christmas. Others insist on strict keeping of the Jewish Sabbath. Verdict: Paul condemns observing days as a requirement for being right with God, as part of the old covenant law. The Old Testament Sabbath was a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). Gathering on the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is not a return to the law, but a privilege of the new covenant (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).
