Christians may also remember events like Christ’s birth and resurrection, as long as these are not made a means of righteousness or bound on others’ consciences.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regular worship is legalism. It means no observance can add to Christ.

In a sentence. You are observing special days and months and seasons and years! Paul fears for you, that somehow he has wasted his efforts on you.

On a Tuesday. Do you rely on religious routines to feel right with God? Rely on Christ alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, I entreat you, become as I am, for I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.

Brothers, I entreat you. Key words. The tone shifts from argument to pleading. “Brothers”: family.

Become as I am. Key words. Free from the law as a way of righteousness.

For I also have become as you are. Key words. Paul, a Jew, lived like a Gentile among them, setting aside Jewish customs (1 Corinthians 9:21). Now he asks them to be free like him.

You did me no wrong. Key words. When he was with them, they treated him well. This is not a personal quarrel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they should copy everything about Paul. It means they should share his freedom in Christ.

In a sentence. Paul pleads with you, brothers and sisters: become like him, for he became like you. You did him no wrong.

For worship. Ask God to make you free in Christ, and to help others be free too.

verseByVerse.quote: You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first, and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.

You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first. Key words. We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes (v. 15; 6:11), others that it was malaria contracted in the lowlands, which drove him to the highlands of Galatia. God used illness to bring Paul to them.

And though my condition was a trial to you. Key words. His condition may have been unpleasant to see. In that culture, some saw illness as a sign of demonic attack or divine displeasure.

You did not scorn or despise me. Key words. “Despise” (ekptyō, literally spit out). Some people spat to ward off evil from the sick. They did not.

But received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. Key words. They welcomed him as God’s messenger, even as Christ himself (Matthew 10:40). They recognised Christ speaking through him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they worshipped Paul. At Lystra, some tried to, and he refused (Acts 14:11–15). It means they received his message as from Christ.

In a sentence. As you know, it was because of an illness that Paul first preached the gospel to you, and even though his illness was a trial to you, you did not treat him with contempt or scorn. Instead, you welcomed him as if he were an angel of God, as if he were Christ Jesus himself.

On a Tuesday. God can use your weakness and illness to bring the gospel to others. Do not despise those who are sick.
verseByVerse.note: We do not know what the illness was; some think it affected his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?

What then has become of your blessedness? Key words. “Blessedness” (makarismos, joy, sense of blessing). Where is the joy they once had in the gospel?

For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me. Key words. They loved him so much they would have given anything. Perhaps a hint that his ailment affected his eyes.

Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth? Key words. Now that he tells them hard truths, do they see him as an enemy? Truth-tellers are often treated as enemies.

What it does not mean. It does not mean feelings of joy prove faith. It means joy in the gospel is lost when we drift from it.

In a sentence. Where, then, is your blessing of me now? Paul can testify that, if you could have done so, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to him. Has he now become your enemy by telling you the truth?

For worship. If you have lost the joy of your salvation, ask God to restore it (Psalm 51:12).

verseByVerse.quote: They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,

They make much of you, but for no good purpose. Key words. “Make much of” (zēloō, court, pay zealous attention to). The false teachers flattered and courted the Galatians. But their motives were selfish.

They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them. Key words. They wanted to exclude the Galatians from Paul and from the true fellowship, so that the Galatians would depend on them and court them in return. Cult-like manipulation.

It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you. Key words. Zeal is good when it is for the right purpose. Paul does not object to their being eagerly sought, but to the motive.

What it does not mean. It does not mean warm attention from others is always manipulative. It means watch the motive.

In a sentence. Those people are zealous to win you over, but for no good. What they want is to alienate you from us, so that you may have zeal for them. It is fine to be zealous, provided the purpose is good, and to be so always, not just when Paul is with you.

On a Tuesday. Beware of teachers who flatter you and try to cut you off from other believers. That is a warning sign.

verseByVerse.quote: my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you! I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.

My little children. Key words. “Little children” (teknia), the only time Paul uses this tender word. A father’s, or mother’s, love.

For whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth. Key words. “Anguish of childbirth” (ōdinō, labour pains). Paul pictures himself as a mother in labour. He went through it once when they were converted; now again.

Until Christ is formed in you! Key words. “Formed” (morphoō, take shape). The goal of all ministry: that Christ’s character takes shape in believers (Romans 8:29; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Not that they look like Paul, or keep the law, but that they look like Christ.

I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone. Key words. Letters are limited. In person he could speak more gently.

For I am perplexed about you. Key words. “Perplexed” (aporeō, at a loss). He does not know what to make of them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they needed to be born again again. Paul’s labour now is for their growth, that Christ be formed.

In a sentence. My dear children, for whom Paul is again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you, how he wishes he could be with you now and change his tone, because he is perplexed about you!

For worship. Pray that Christ will be formed in you, and in those you love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — Hagar and Sarah: Two Covenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the story of Abraham’s two sons, one by the slave woman Hagar, born in the ordinary way, and one by the free woman Sarah, born by promise. He reads them as two covenants: Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery with her children; Sarah stands for the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother, as Isaiah promised the barren woman many children. Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise. As the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit then, so it is now. Scripture says to drive out the slave woman and her son, so believers are children not of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.theology:
Typology, and Why the Two Covenants Cannot Share a House

Verse 24 is not allegory in the Alexandrian sense that dissolves history. Paul’s premise is that it is written that Abraham had two sons; he treats the mothers, the statuses and the manner of each birth as facts. He is saying the history happened and was designed to carry a meaning the coming of Christ has made visible — which is what the risen Christ himself did on the Emmaus road (Lk. 24:27). If God governs history, a pattern in a true story is not imposed by the reader; it is put there by the author.

Verses 24–25 supply the test that governs the whole section: what a covenant produces tells you what kind of covenant it is. Sinai was genuinely from God and still bore children for slavery, because that was its office. And v. 30 states the reason a mixture is impossible. Add merit to grace and the result is not a moderate position but merit, since the moment performance is part of the ground the whole weight has moved onto it. Two guards belong with v. 30: Paul casts out a system, not persons — he is in labour pains for the people who hold it — and Genesis itself has God hearing Ishmael in the desert and being with him as he grew (Gen. 21:17–20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers presented themselves as the true heirs of Abraham. Verse 22 shows that blood was never the mechanism, v. 23 that the difference lay in how each son came to exist, and vv. 24–25 place the Jerusalem establishment on the slave woman’s side. Verse 29 then explains why religious men were persecuting a Gentile church: a man who has spent his life earning his standing cannot hear that a farmer who believed last month is equally accepted, because it writes off the investment. The elder brother of Luke 15:29–30 says nothing untrue about himself and is furious.

Now:Verse 23 finds most readers before the Judaizers do: the situation you have decided you must arrange yourself because God is taking too long is Hagar’s tent. And v. 29 is a warning before it is a comfort: watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.

Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law? Key words. The law here means the books of Moses, the Torah, including Genesis. If you want the law, hear what the law says.

For it is written that Abraham had two sons. Key words. Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by his free wife Sarah was Isaac (Genesis 16; 21).

One by a slave woman and one by a free woman. Key words. The mothers’ status determined the sons’ status.

But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh. Key words. Ishmael was born by natural means, by human planning, when Abraham and Sarah tried to fulfil God’s promise their own way (Genesis 16:1–4).

While the son of the free woman was born through promise. Key words. Isaac was born by God’s supernatural power to a barren old woman, as God promised (Genesis 18:10–14; 21:1–2). Human effort versus God’s promise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God had no care for Ishmael. He blessed him (Genesis 21:13, 17–21). But Ishmael was not the heir of the covenant.

In a sentence. Tell Paul, you who want to be under the law, are you not aware of what the law says? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman. His son by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, but his son by the free woman was born as the result of a divine promise.

For worship. If you are a believer, you were born by God’s promise and power, like Isaac. Thank him.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham’s son by the slave woman Hagar was Ishmael; his son by the free woman Sarah was Isaac, born by promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

Now this may be interpreted allegorically. Key words. “Allegorically” (allēgoreō, speak another way, figuratively). Paul draws a deeper spiritual meaning from the historical story.

These women are two covenants. Key words. Hagar and Sarah represent two covenants.

One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar. Key words. The covenant of law, given at Sinai. Those who rely on it as the way to righteousness are slaves.

Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia. Key words. Sinai was in Arabia, the land of Hagar’s descendants, the Ishmaelites.

She corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children. Key words. Shocking for Jews: the earthly Jerusalem, centre of Judaism, which rejected Christ and clung to the law, is in slavery like Hagar.

Where Christians differ: allegory in interpretation. Some use this passage to justify reading allegories into all of Scripture, finding hidden meanings unrelated to the plain sense. Verdict: Paul’s method here is closer to typology than to free allegory. He does not deny the history; he sees in real events a pattern God built into history that points forward to the gospel (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). Interpreters should first grasp the plain meaning of a text, and only find further meanings where Scripture itself warrants them. Paul, writing under inspiration, had that warrant; later interpreters must stay within what Scripture teaches.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish people are rejected by God. Paul speaks of the system of law apart from Christ.

In a sentence. These things are being taken figuratively: the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children who are to be slaves: this is Hagar. Now Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present city of Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament looking for the patterns that point to Christ. But start with what the text plainly says.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”

But the Jerusalem above is free. Key words. The heavenly Jerusalem: the city of God, the true people of God, the new covenant (Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2). Believers already belong to it.

And she is our mother. Key words. Corresponding to Sarah. Believers are children of the free woman, born from above.

For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor!” Key words. From Isaiah 54:1, a promise to Jerusalem in exile, desolate like a barren woman. God would give her more children than ever.

“For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.” Key words. Paul sees this fulfilled in the church: Sarah, barren, became the mother of a multitude; the new Jerusalem, including Gentiles from every nation, has countless children.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church replaces Israel entirely. Jewish believers are part of the Jerusalem above too.

In a sentence. But the Jerusalem that is above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written: “Be glad, barren woman, you who never bore a child; shout for joy and cry aloud, you who were never in labour; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.”

For worship. You belong to the free city above. Rejoice with all its countless children.

parallels.desc: sing, O barren one, who did not bear

verseByVerse.quote: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.

Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. Key words. The Gentile Galatians, born by God’s promise and Spirit, are like Isaac.

But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit. Key words. Ishmael mocked Isaac (Genesis 21:9). Jewish tradition expanded this into persecution. Born according to the Spirit: Isaac’s birth by God’s power.

So also it is now. Key words. The false teachers, relying on the flesh, were persecuting those who trust in the Spirit. Those who rely on human effort often oppose those who rely on grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution justifies hatred in return. Believers bless those who persecute them.

In a sentence. Now you, brothers and sisters, like Isaac, are children of promise. At that time the son born according to the flesh persecuted the son born by the power of the Spirit. It is the same now.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for trusting grace, do not be surprised. Isaac was too.

verseByVerse.quote: But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.

But what does the Scripture say? Key words. Scripture settles it.

“Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” Key words. Sarah’s words in Genesis 21:10, which God confirmed (Genesis 21:12). Law-religion and grace cannot share the inheritance. The Galatians should cast out the false teachers and their message.

So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman. Key words. The conclusion. Believers are free children of promise, heirs of everything. This leads into 5:1: for freedom Christ has set us free.

What it does not mean. It does not mean cruelty to people. It means refusing to mix law-righteousness with grace.

In a sentence. But what does Scripture say? “Get rid of the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman’s son.” Therefore, brothers and sisters, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.

For worship. Thank God that you are a free child of promise. Refuse every voice that would bring you back into slavery.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman with her son

5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the hinge on which the entire letter turns from theology to life. The freedom Paul has argued for throughout — freedom from the law as a system of justification, freedom from the curse, freedom from the elementary principles of the old age — must now be shown to produce not moral chaos but something far better than law-keeping ever could. The chapter answers two questions that the letter’s argument raises: What does this freedom look like in practice? And what is its alternative to the law as the shaping force of Christian behavior?

The answer to the first question is given negatively and positively. Negatively: freedom is not license (“do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh”). The Judaizers’ accusation — that a gospel without law-requirements would produce moral anarchy — is not left unanswered. But the answer is not to reinstate the law; the answer is to walk in the Spirit. Positively: the whole law is fulfilled in one word — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (v. 14). Those who walk by the Spirit do not need the law to produce love, because the Spirit is the Spirit of the God who is love, and his fruit in the believer is love. The Judaizers’ program produced biting and devouring; the Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

The heart of the chapter is the contrast between the works of the flesh (vv. 19–21) and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 22–23). The language itself is instructive: works (plural, produced by human striving) versus fruit (singular, the organic product of the Spirit’s life within). The flesh produces a catalogue of self-serving, community-destroying behaviors; the Spirit produces a coherent, integrated character that is nothing less than the character of Christ. The goal of the Christian life is not the avoidance of the flesh’s works by rule-keeping but the cultivation of the Spirit’s life by staying close to the one who gives it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 compresses four chapters into a line: for freedom Christ has set us free. The apparent tautology is the point — freedom is the destination, not a stage on the way to a stricter religion. Stand firm is a military verb, because freedom is not a resting state; slavery is restful in a way liberty is not, since a slave always knows where he stands. The yoke of slavery is Peter’s own phrase for the law at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:10), and it sits against the yoke Jesus offers in Matthew 11:29–30. Nobody goes without a yoke; the question is whose.

Verses 2–3 are the warning. If a man accepts circumcision as what completes his standing, Christ is of no advantage to him — not less, none, because he has changed systems into one that has no column for what somebody else has done. Verse 3 closes the escape route: he is obligated to keep the whole law, not the one item he was sold. Verse 4 states the result in two phrases that describe a change of position rather than of behaviour: severed from Christ, fallen out of the sphere of grace. Verse 5 draws the line with an emphatic we ourselves, and adds the note of waiting; v. 6 says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts, but faith working through love.

Then the appeal. Verse 7 uses a technical word for cutting in on a runner — somebody stepped into their lane. Verse 8 says quietly that this persuasion is not from him who calls them. Verse 9 warns that a little leaven changes the whole loaf, invisibly, while it is happening. Verse 10 is the surprise: Paul is confident about them, in the Lord, and leaves the troubler to God. Verse 11 shows what was being said about him and names the offence of the cross, and v. 12 aims a deliberately shocking wish at teachers who make the knife the mechanism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

The Reformed tradition has always held that gospel freedom is more than freedom from sin’s penalty; it is freedom from performance-based religion — liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. This is not antinomianism. The law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk in the Spirit rather than imposed from without on those who must earn a standing. Luther’s paradox holds both: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.

Verse 4 must be read for what it says. Both its clauses describe position, not conduct: the people addressed have become more religious, not less, and Paul identifies them in the same breath as those who would be justified by the law. To fall from grace here is to step off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, where Christ’s work is inoperative — not to have disgraced oneself, which is the phrase’s modern and quite different meaning. That Paul writes v. 10 six sentences later, expressing confidence about the very same people, settles how v. 4 is functioning: it is the warning that prevents the thing it describes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade — a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it is not an upgrade but an exchange, and v. 3 reads them the rest of the contract nobody mentioned. Verse 11 reveals that Paul was being quoted against himself, perhaps on the strength of his past; his answer is his scars. Verse 12 would have landed with local force, since the mother goddess, whose chief shrine was at Pessinus, was served by priests who castrated themselves.

Now:Standing firm (v. 1) usually means refusing to answer “where do I stand with God today?” by reaching for the last few days. Verse 4 describes a man at peace with being justified by his own record, which is the opposite of the reader it frightens; and v. 8 gives a usable test for any new teaching — does it come to you the way the God who called you came to you?

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.

Meaning first. Galatians 5 turns from argument to application: what does freedom in Christ mean in practice? First, stand firm in it. To accept circumcision as necessary for salvation would be to abandon Christ and fall from grace; believers wait for the hope of righteousness by faith through the Spirit, and what counts is faith working through love (vv. 1–12). Second, freedom is not licence. Believers are called to freedom, but not to indulge the flesh; rather to serve one another in love, which fulfils the law (vv. 13–15). Third, the way to live free is to walk by the Spirit. The flesh and the Spirit are at war within the believer. The works of the flesh are obvious, from sexual immorality to envy and drunkenness, and those who live by them will not inherit the kingdom. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh; so let them keep in step with the Spirit (vv. 16–26).

For freedom Christ has set us free. Key words. The purpose of Christ’s work: freedom (eleutheria). Freedom from the law as a way of righteousness, from its curse, from sin’s slavery, and freedom to live for God. Christ did not free us so that we could become slaves again.

Stand firm therefore. Key words. “Stand firm” (stēkō, hold your ground). Freedom must be defended.

And do not submit again to a yoke of slavery. Key words. A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals: a picture of burden and servitude. The rabbis spoke of the yoke of the law as a good thing; Peter called it a yoke neither we nor our fathers could bear (Acts 15:10). Jesus offers his easy yoke instead (Matthew 11:29–30).

What it does not mean. It does not mean freedom to do whatever we like. Verse 13 rules that out.

In a sentence. It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery.

On a Tuesday. Are there religious rules you have taken on as if they made you more acceptable to God? Lay them down, and stand in Christ’s freedom.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals — a picture of burdensome obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.

Look: I, Paul, say to you. Key words. Emphatic, with full apostolic authority.

That if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. Key words. If they are circumcised as a requirement for salvation, they are trusting in law-keeping, not Christ. Christ plus circumcision equals Christ of no value. You cannot have Christ as a partial Saviour.

I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law. Key words. Circumcision is not a one-off ritual; it signs you up to the whole law (James 2:10). If you choose the law, you must keep all of it, perfectly. No one can.

What it does not mean. It does not mean circumcision as a medical or cultural practice is sinful. Paul circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3). He speaks of circumcision as a requirement for righteousness.

In a sentence. Mark Paul’s words! He, Paul, tells you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all. Again he declares to every man who lets himself be circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law.

For worship. Christ is all-sufficient. Do not add anything to him. Rest in his finished work.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.

You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law. Key words. “Severed” (katargeō, cut off, separated, made void). Seeking justification by the law means cutting yourself off from Christ. You cannot hold on to both.

You have fallen away from grace. Key words. “Fallen away” (ekpiptō, fallen out of). To fall from grace is not to fall into sin, as people often think, but to fall into law-righteousness: leaving the sphere of grace for the sphere of works.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall from grace? Some take this verse to mean true believers can lose their salvation. Verdict: Paul is describing the meaning and consequence of seeking justification by law: it is a rejection of grace and Christ. Those who persist in it show they never truly rested on Christ (1 John 2:19). True believers may be confused and tempted, as the Galatians were, but God keeps his own (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29), and warnings like this one are among his means of keeping them. Falling from grace here means abandoning the principle of grace, not a true believer being lost.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sinning makes you fall from grace. Grace is for sinners.

In a sentence. You who are trying to be justified by the law have been alienated from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.

On a Tuesday. Falling from grace is not sinning; it is trying to earn God’s favour. Stay in grace.

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.

For through the Spirit, by faith. Key words. The Christian way: the Spirit, received by faith.

We ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. Key words. “Eagerly wait” (apekdechomai). The hope of righteousness: the final verdict of acquittal at the judgement, the full revelation of our righteousness in Christ. Believers are already justified (Romans 5:1), and wait confidently for that verdict to be publicly declared.

For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything. Key words. Ethnic and religious markers are irrelevant to standing with God.

But only faith working through love. Key words. “Working” (energeō, operating, energised). True faith is never idle; it shows itself in love. Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

Where Christians differ: faith working through love. Roman Catholic teaching has used this phrase to argue that we are justified by faith formed by love, so that love is part of the ground of justification. Verdict: Paul says what counts is faith, and describes that faith as one that works through love. Love is the fruit of justifying faith, not part of its ground. We are justified by faith alone, receiving Christ’s righteousness; the faith that receives Christ then works through love (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17; Westminster 11.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith without works can save. Dead faith is not saving faith. It means works are the fruit, not the root.

In a sentence. For through the Spirit we eagerly await by faith the righteousness for which we hope. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. The only thing that counts is faith expressing itself through love.

For worship. Thank God for justifying faith. Ask him to make your faith show itself in love today.

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.

You were running well. Key words. A race picture. They started the Christian life well.

Who hindered you from obeying the truth? Key words. “Hindered” (enkoptō, cut in, as a runner cutting across another’s lane). Someone tripped them up. Obeying the truth: believing and living the gospel.

This persuasion is not from him who calls you. Key words. God, who called them by grace, is not the source of this new teaching.

A little leaven leavens the whole lump. Key words. Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough (1 Corinthians 5:6). A small addition to the gospel corrupts the whole. False teaching, though it starts small, spreads.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every small disagreement corrupts the church. It means adding to the gospel, even a little, is deadly.

In a sentence. You were running a good race. Who cut in on you to keep you from obeying the truth? That kind of persuasion does not come from the one who calls you. A little yeast works through the whole batch of dough.

On a Tuesday. Watch for small compromises in the gospel. They spread.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!

I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view. Key words. Paul trusts that God will bring them back.

And the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. Key words. God will judge the false teacher, however important.

But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Key words. Some claimed Paul himself preached circumcision when it suited him (perhaps because of Timothy). If so, why do Jews still persecute him?

In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. Key words. “Offence” (skandalon, stumbling block). The cross offends because it says we can contribute nothing to our salvation. Add circumcision, and the offence disappears, because human pride is satisfied. The gospel of grace always offends human pride.

I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves! Key words. Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele, popular in Galatia, who castrated themselves. If they are so keen on cutting, let them go the whole way, and become like pagan priests. Strong words, showing how seriously Paul takes the danger.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may use crude insults freely. Paul’s language reflects the extreme danger to souls.

In a sentence. Paul is confident in the Lord that you will take no other view. The one who is throwing you into confusion, whoever that may be, will have to pay the penalty. Brothers and sisters, if he is still preaching circumcision, why is he still being persecuted? In that case the offence of the cross has been abolished. As for those agitators, he wishes they would go the whole way and castrate themselves!

For worship. Do not try to remove the offence of the cross. Preach it as it is.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele in that region, who castrated themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They were called to freedom, but they must not use it as an excuse for the flesh; instead they should serve one another in love. The whole law is summed up in one command, to love your neighbour as yourself. If they bite and devour one another, they will be destroyed by each other.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

The relation of law and love in Reformed ethics is exact. The law’s moral demands are not abolished for the believer; they are fulfilled, but from a different source and in a different direction. The law compels from outside and leaves the sinner exposed; love, produced by the Spirit, constrains from within and overflows. This is what the older divines meant by the law written on the heart (Jer. 31:33) — not a different law, but the same law internalised by the Spirit of adoption and obeyed as the expression of a heart that loves the God who gave everything, rather than as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also settles the charge of antinomianism that has followed the doctrine of free grace since the first century. Paul concedes the danger frankly and then refuses the remedy his opponents wanted. That refusal is the test of whether a man has understood the gospel he preaches: it is easy to answer licence with law, and it undoes everything. And v. 15 exposes the mechanism by which a doctrine of performance destroys a congregation — once standing is earned, every other believer becomes a measurement, and the resulting suspicion has a righteous vocabulary to conduct itself in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy, which is not an irony but a mechanism. The very community the Judaizers claimed to be perfecting by law-observance was tearing itself apart, and vv. 13–14 name the only thing that binds a church in the way rules never can.

Now:A church that makes the Christian life primarily about observable markers will always produce the same social weather: pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, comparison, and division. The cure v. 13 offers is not a new rule but service, given concretely to the person you are still disagreeing with.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

For you were called to freedom, brothers. Key words. God called them into freedom.

Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Key words. “Opportunity” (aphormē, a base of operations, a launching point). Freedom must not become a base for sin. The flesh: sinful human nature.

But through love serve one another. Key words. “Serve” (douleuō, be slaves). Ironic and beautiful: freed from slavery to the law, believers become slaves of one another in love. True freedom is freedom to love.

For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Key words. From Leviticus 19:18 (Romans 13:8–10). Love fulfils what the law commanded. Those who walk by the Spirit in love do what the law required, not to be justified, but as its fruit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love replaces the commandments, so that we decide what love means. Love is defined by the commandments (Romans 13:9).

In a sentence. You, brothers and sisters, were called to be free. But do not use your freedom to indulge the flesh; rather, serve one another humbly in love. For the entire law is fulfilled in keeping this one command: “Love your neighbour as yourself.”

On a Tuesday. Use your freedom today to serve someone in love.

parallels.desc: you shall love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

But if you bite and devour one another. Key words. Like wild animals fighting. The controversy in Galatia had turned the churches into battlegrounds.

Watch out that you are not consumed by one another. Key words. Churches can destroy themselves through infighting. Legalism often produces harsh criticism of others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean truth does not matter. Paul fights hard for it in this letter. It means believers must not attack each other with cruelty.

In a sentence. If you bite and devour each other, watch out or you will be destroyed by each other.

For worship. Ask God to forgive any biting words you have spoken against fellow believers. Make peace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to walk by the Spirit, and they will not carry out the desires of the flesh, for the two are opposed and at war within them. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law. The works of the flesh are plain: sexual sin, impurity, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousy, rage, rivalry, divisions, envy, drunkenness and the like, and those who live this way will not inherit God’s kingdom. The Spirit produces a very different harvest: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, against which no law stands. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions. Since they live by the Spirit, they should keep in step with him, and not become conceited, provoking or envying one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification and Vivification, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

Reformed theology has always described the Christian life as two complementary movements: mortification, the putting to death of the flesh, which v. 24 states as something already done to every believer; and vivification, the coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The mortification is the application to daily life of what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the vivification is the fruit of the Spirit’s indwelling. The believer does not produce either. He participates in both by faith.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image itself. Crucifixion was chosen by Rome precisely because it was slow: a man nailed to a beam was mortally wounded, fixed, going nowhere — and still perfectly capable of shouting. That is the flesh in a believer. Its authority is broken and its outcome settled, and it will go on being audible until the body dies. Verse 21 must be read with the same care. Scripture never confuses a man who falls into a ditch with a man who lives in it, and the ache that makes a tender conscience afraid of that verse is itself the evidence the verse is not describing him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third. Verse 20 would have been the most uncomfortable line in the letter read aloud in those congregations, since the middle of Paul’s list of fleshly works is a description of what was happening in the room. Verse 25 carries a piece of quiet artistry: stoichōmen, keep in step, is built on the same root as the stoicheia that had them in bondage in 4:3 and 4:9. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

Now:Walking by the Spirit (v. 16) is concrete rather than mystical: asking before the difficult conversation rather than after it, going where he speaks often enough to know his voice, and obeying the small prompt you would rather not have noticed. And v. 26 has a test anyone can run: what happens in you when good news is announced about the believer whose life is flourishing most visibly?

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

But I say, walk by the Spirit. Key words. The answer to both legalism and licence. “Walk” (peripateō): live, conduct yourself, step by step. By the Spirit: depending on him, following his lead, relying on his power.

And you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. Key words. A promise: walking by the Spirit means not carrying out the flesh’s desires. “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh. Key words. A war within every believer. The flesh still wants its way; the Spirit opposes it.

For these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. Key words. The struggle means believers cannot simply do whatever they want, whether good or evil, without opposition.

But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. Key words. Led (agō), as in Romans 8:14. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law’s condemnation or as a system of control. They fulfil it from within.

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some teach that believers can reach a state where the flesh is eradicated and they no longer sin. Verdict: Paul describes an ongoing war between flesh and Spirit in the believer. The Spirit gives real victory, and believers grow in holiness, but the flesh is not destroyed until glory (Romans 7:14–25; 1 John 1:8; Westminster 13.2). The Christian life is a fight, not a state of sinless rest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are helpless. The Spirit is stronger, and walking by him brings victory.

In a sentence. So Paul says, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are in conflict with each other, so that you are not to do whatever you want. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

On a Tuesday. When you feel the pull of the flesh today, stop and pray: Holy Spirit, lead me.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

Now the works of the flesh are evident. Key words. “Evident” (phanera, obvious, plain). Works: what the flesh produces. Fifteen are listed in four groups.

Sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality. Key words. Sexual sins. Sexual immorality (porneia): all sex outside marriage. Impurity (akatharsia): moral uncleanness. Sensuality (aselgeia): open, shameless indulgence.

Idolatry, sorcery. Key words. Religious sins. “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs (pharmakeia, from which pharmacy). Common in Galatia.

Enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy. Key words. Eight sins of relationships, the largest group. Enmity (hostility), strife (quarrelling), jealousy, fits of anger (outbursts of rage), rivalries (selfish ambition), dissensions (splits), divisions (factions, haireseis), envy. These were tearing the Galatian churches apart (v. 15). Respectable church people commit these.

Drunkenness, orgies. Key words. Sins of excess. Orgies (kōmoi, wild partying).

And things like these. Key words. The list is not complete.

I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. Key words. “Do” (prassō, practise, present tense): those whose lives are characterised by these. Not the believer who falls and repents, but the one who continues in them without repentance (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a single sin excludes a believer from the kingdom. It means a life ruled by the flesh shows a person is not ruled by the Spirit.

In a sentence. The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity and debauchery; idolatry and witchcraft; hatred, discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissensions, factions and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. Paul warns you, as he did before, that those who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God.

For worship. Look honestly at this list. Confess the works of the flesh you see in yourself, and turn to Christ for cleansing.
verseByVerse.note: “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.

But the fruit of the Spirit. Key words. “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours. The works of the flesh are many and fragmented; the fruit of the Spirit is one, a whole character. Fruit grows naturally from life; it is not manufactured. The Spirit produces it as we abide in Christ (John 15:4–5).

Is love. Key words. Agapē: self-giving love. First, and the root of the rest (1 Corinthians 13).

Joy, peace. Key words. Joy (chara): gladness in God, independent of circumstances. Peace (eirēnē): wholeness, rest in God, harmony with others.

Patience, kindness, goodness. Key words. Patience (makrothymia, long-suffering): bearing with others. Kindness (chrēstotēs): gracious tenderness. Goodness (agathōsynē): active moral excellence and generosity.

Faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Key words. Faithfulness (pistis): reliability, loyalty. Gentleness (prautēs): meekness, strength under control. Self-control (enkrateia): mastery over desires.

Against such things there is no law. Key words. No law forbids these. The Spirit-filled life more than fulfils the law. This is a portrait of Christ himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are passive. They must sow to the Spirit (6:8) and keep in step with him (v. 25). But the growth is his work.

In a sentence. But the fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

On a Tuesday. Pick one fruit of the Spirit you most lack. Pray for it today, and look for one chance to show it.
verseByVerse.note: “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

And those who belong to Christ Jesus. Key words. All true believers.

Have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Key words. Past tense: a decisive act at conversion. United to Christ in his death, believers put the flesh to death (2:20; Romans 6:6). They turned decisively against their sinful nature. Crucifixion was slow, painful and final. The flesh still struggles, but it has been condemned. Now believers continue to put it to death daily (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the flesh no longer troubles believers. Verse 17 shows it does. It means its power has been broken and its doom sealed.

In a sentence. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

For worship. Thank Christ that in union with him, your old self has been crucified. Live in that victory.

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

If we live by the Spirit. Key words. If the Spirit gives us life, as he does all believers.

Let us also keep in step with the Spirit. Key words. “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line (stoicheō). Follow the Spirit’s lead step by step, in daily obedience, as soldiers follow the one ahead. Being indicative becomes command: you have the Spirit, so walk with him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean waiting for feelings or inner voices. The Spirit leads mainly through his word.

In a sentence. Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Ask: what is my next step of obedience to the Spirit today? Take it.
verseByVerse.note: “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

Let us not become conceited. Key words. “Conceited” (kenodoxos, empty glory, vainglory). Pride in spiritual achievements.

Provoking one another. Key words. “Provoking” (prokaleomai, challenging, as to a fight). Those who feel spiritually superior provoke others.

Envying one another. Key words. Those who feel inferior envy others. Pride and envy are two sides of the same comparison. The Spirit frees us from both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we may not encourage one another to good works (Hebrews 10:24). It means no competing.

In a sentence. Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying each other.

On a Tuesday. Stop comparing yourself with other Christians. Neither look down nor look up enviously. Look to Christ.
